9.title: Oozing with originality
9.content:
This is a world where people can go into your dreams. Some are even able to use your dreams to influence your actions. Dom Cobb (Leonardo DiCaprio) is skilled at stealing secrets by diving into your dreams. It's a dark treacherous world where he has made too many enemies. Now he is offered a chance to come in from the cold. This time his team is tasked to plant an idea into the target's mind, or in one word inception.

Christopher Nolan has created something of a Penrose-stairs structure in this movie. It's complicated and may be too convoluted to be reasonable. But that's as much part of its charm. The worlds, the effects, the ideas are all first rate. It is oozing with originality.

The actors are also first rate. Nolan can command the best cast to his projects now. There is nobody better than DiCaprio to anchor this movie. Nothing about this movie is done with lesser parts. This is indeed a top movie.

9.title: Mazed and Confused
9.content:
Greetings again from the darkness. Some movies are made as pure visual entertainment. Others are made as a vision of a story. The best combine elements of both. The great ones WOW you with what you see on screen, while keeping your mind focused on the multiple dimensions of a story that just won't let you get ahead. The previous sentence is my feeble attempt at describing what happens during "Inception".

Writer/director Christopher Nolan turns 40 at the end of this month. He now has 3 instant-classic films to his credit: "Memento", "The Dark Knight" and now "Inception". I am not a good enough writer to describe just how talented he his at making films. What I can tell you is that this movie gave me a "runner's high" ... it put me "in the zone". As a viewer, I felt in perfect sync at each twist and turn.

There are two pieces of advice I will offer. First, go see the film at a theatre on the big screen. Don't wait for NetFlix. Second, pay attention to every scene and every line. Trust Mr. Nolan to take you on this wild ride. You may be able to figure out the ending (if there even is one), but you will have missed the real point of the film ... how did you get here? Here is a brief synopsis: Leonardo DiCaprio plays an expert thief. He is a thief who steals ideas by infiltrating the dreams of his targets and snatching their ideas. A very wealthy tycoon played by Ken Watanabe hires DiCaprio for a risky project of Inception - the inserting of an idea into the subject's mind through dreams, rather than the stealing of an idea. DiCaprio's team is played by Joseph Gordon-Levitt (with physical brilliance while lacking gravitational force), Tom Hardy (from Rocknrolla), master chemist Dileep Rao, and new recruit Ellen Page (Juno plays a brilliant architect prodigy with a genius of space and dimension). Cillian Murphy plays the target and Michael Caine is DiCaprio's father in law ... the link between who Leo is now and his previous life with his wife, played hauntingly well by Marion Cotillard.

A perfect Nolan touch is Ellen Page's character name - Ariadne. A quick google finds that Ariadne, in Greek mythology, fell in love with Theseus and helped him escape Minotaur's labyrinth. The film is full of mazes and is itself a labyrinth punctuated by a stunning and powerful score by Hans Zimmer. You will find yourself bouncing from dream to reality, jumping into another's dreams, layering dreams upon each other ... oh, and watching a mind-bending special effect as the city of Paris is folded over on top of itself.

Clear your mind for 2 and a half hours and let a terrific filmmaker take you on a journey through mindspace that we never really pay attention to. The payoff is dream-like.

9.title: Christopher Nolan's Greatest Achievement
9.content:
When first hearing of Inception and it's intriguing plot, I was automatically interested. Eventually, that interest transformed into an irresistible urge to watch it. When I did view this movie, I was amazed at the complexity of the story line (although before watching it I figured it would be) and the exceptional amount of thought put into this movie.

When watching this movie I saw immediately realized the depth and complexity of Inception, which most people fail to recognize in such a movie. In my humble opinion, this is Christopher Nolan's greatest achievement, although, to grasp the deepest complexities and concepts it is imperative that you heed close attention throughout the entire duration of the movie; failure to do such will result in confusion and or watching the movie again to actually grasp it (as required for many of my own friends).

To any individual with an above average intellect, I highly recommend this movie to you, any other individuals, stick with the Disney movies.

9.title: I bought the airline. Awesome movie.
9.content:
My Score: 9.0/10

I need to quote what one of my colleague always says: "This is absolutely BONKERS". This movie is... simply amazing, creative and decent.

This is a science-fiction movie with its background set very similar to our modern days world. Dom Cobb (starred by Leonardo DiCaprio) was a skilled thief, who specialized in extracting and stealing valuable secrets from within the subconscious during the dream state of his targets. Having failed one of his missions Cobb and his partner, Arthur were captured but been offered another chance to redeem themselves. However instead of stealing from dreams, they were asked to carry out a seemingly-impossible mission: To implant an idea in their target's dreams (the so-called "Inception"). The story went on to see how Cobb assembled his team for the mission, and at the same time battle his own struggles in his own subconsciousness, in which he has lost his beloved wife.

Firstly, the idea of the movie is very creative. The basic concept is about layers of dream, as you drill down the layers they become more and more unstable due to the states of our human brain. I think it is already very creative to describe about "a dream inside a dream", but I never expected the director and producers could go so far into describing as many as 4 layers of dreams! Secondly, I think the use of angles and camera shots have brought movie-viewing into yet another new level. The viewing sensation is so strong and well-captured that you feel the intensity inside the dreams at every moment. Thirdly, the strong cast have given a hard core performance. I especially want to mention Leonardo DiCaprio who portrayed so well as a mentally-exhausted man, who wanted so much to redeem himself and go back home. I have regarded him as an impressive actor since his performance in "Blood Diamond".

Despite a rather straight-forward storyline and no totally unexpected twists, personally it is understandable as audience may already find it difficult in following the interactions between different layers of dream. I think this movie can be even more complicated than "The Matrix" but it chose to tell its story in a most viewer-friendly way, which I greatly appreciated as an audience.

In summary, a highly recommended movie that you should not miss in August 2010.

p.s I really liked the moment when Saito said "I bought the airline". That is what I call "cool".

9.title: A film to remember
9.content:
Why did give this movie 10/10? Simply because of it's originality, it's script and it's direction. Inception is one of the great cinematic works that you must experience for itself. You may have to see it twice to fully grasp it's complex plot, but you even have to solve the puzzle for yourself to understand and appreciate a script that has taken nine years to write. I only hope it gets the Oscar nominations it deserves.

And it does deserve a hell of a lot of nominations. I predict it will win best screenplay but other wins are likely. Leonardo Di Caprio was the perfect actor in my opinion to play as the main character. He brings mystery, intelligence and believable action to the plot. A must see film!

9.title: It's like REVOLVER but even better!
9.content:
I hate missing the start of movies and one I rally didn't want to miss the start of was INCEPTION (2010). That I did was frustrating, not only did it put me ill at ease, unaware of how much had taken place, but I was worried that what I'd heard was such a complex film would be impossible to catch up with. Thankfully confusion led to clarity and I was able to enjoy ever moment of this fast-paced psychological thriller.

The ideas were complicated but the format was quite simple really, you'd get some exposition, explaining the "rules" of this world or revealing information about the lead character, then a grand action sequence. This formula was then repeated over two hours. Conversational scenes provided a lot of information to think about and the action scenes were very exciting.

As absurd as the film is conceptually it was impossible for me to be bored and remarkable that it could be played so straight. I think that that's one of the tricks and points of the film. In a dream anything, no matter how bizarre, can be accepted as real. Nolan's film is an attempt to create a shared dream-like experience, to draw us in and make the unbelievable believable. He toyed with a similar idea in THE PRESTIGE (2006).

Of course as this is a movie about dreams it inevitably opens up similar questions to less bombastic films exploring reality and fantasy. The likes of DONNIE DARKO (2001), REVOLVER (2005) and THE FOUNTAIN (2006) were all deliberately complex and provoked discussion. But Nolan's film, while challenging, is much more straight-forward.

The core narrative is that of a heist film, the characters are con artists, the action scenes are gunfights, foot chases, car chases, explosions and many other things with which we are familiar. Even the idea of shared dreams isn't new. I think this familiarity allows us to connect with the film and accept its fantasy much more easily. The technology that allows shared dreaming is seen in passing and only casually referenced but we accept it and move with the story.

Even the last job/mission plotting is little more than a familiar framework to engage us, with the "idea" (to be inserted into the mark's mind) little more than a McGuffin. This is a simple story told with complexity, just as with REVOLVER.

The lead (played by Leonardo DiCaprio) is a criminal who has escaped arrest and cannot return to his home and his family but desperately wants to do so. His motivation in taking this job/mission is that very prospect and it's his journey and not the action movie mechanics that are the real point and this is what makes the ending (in particular what the director shows us in the final shot) something to ponder.

Was it all a dream? Beyond that basic thought I hadn't initially given much thought to Inception's ending. But after looking at the comments online it got me thinking a lot.

The film definitely speaks to people on various levels, enough to write many essays on, but I don't think it's as complicated as many people are suggesting.

In this kind of movie the latter is the easiest to go with. It's that USUAL SUSPECTS (1995) reaction. It could be that all the supporting characters were "projections" created by the lead's subconscious to help him deal with regret and grief, resolved at the conclusion. But if you think about it this idea doesn't really go anywhere because of the ending's ambiguity. It could have been an interesting and very conclusive ending had, for example, DiCaprio's character been seen waking up without his colleagues, perhaps at home and then going to play with his children.

I'm intrigued by the idea that perhaps Mal didn't die, that they really were still dreaming when she killed herself and that he was stuck there without her, convinced it was reality. Going through the journey so that he can adapt his dream reality to this loss, to get over his grief and becoming happy with his imagined children. All the time unaware he's still sleeping. Is this tragic? Deep in his subconscious time may stretch but surely he'll wake up at some point and they will be reunited. This essentially renders the whole film pointless and there is no real reward in that interpretation.

Probably the simplest interpretation is that it was only the final part of the movie that was a dream. That the mission was a success but our hero has become lost in his own subconscious despite having resolved his issues. A tragic happy ending that leaves us to ponder what might happen when he really does awaken.

9.title: Inception - Very good, although not my movie of the year
9.content:
The essence of a movie can usually be described in one sentence, which gives you enough information to get a feeling what the movie is about. This sentence has been formed based on an idea. When that idea has been thought up the script writer start expanding on it. Together with set builders and many other people involved in preparation they are the architects who create the world in which the movie will be set. This can be a single room or many locations, anything is possible.

When preparation is done the director and actors step into the world and take care in filling in all the small details. They do this by improvising, making changes to scenes or shooting it a specific way. All this takes places within the confines of the concept for the movie.

When the movie finally has been edited, it's up to the person that goes to the cinema to step into this temporary reality. If the movie is a good one you'll disappear in it, the world around you no longer exists and you forget that you are sitting in a chair at the cinema. You are actually in the place that is shown on the screen. The ending of the movie is the shock that takes you back to reality. If the movie was powerful and had some messages that resonate with your own ideas they might even become part of your own values. If that's the case, the whole team behind making the movie has made a masterpiece.

Inception uses this concept, but instead of movies they use this on dreams. Christopher Nolan ( Following, Memento, Insomnia, Batman Begins, The Prestige and The Dark Knight) shows his vision on what's possible in your dreams, but has he managed to create a masterpiece? When you take a look at Nolan's previous movies, you'll come to the conclusion that he has managed to deliver quality movies. After the success of the new Batman movies he has managed to make his mark as one of the top directors in Hollywood and has been given the opportunity and money to make Inception.

Inception is about a team of thieves that do their work in the dreams of their victims. So their goal is not to steal money or other physical things, but to get their "hands" on thoughts or ideas the person has, which they can then deliver to whoever hired them. Of course this is the ultimate way to do industrial espionage and the team is asked by a company's top executive if they are able to plant an idea in the mind of one of his competitors. The team is not sure that this is even possible, but still decide to take the assignment.

The setup is comparable to other heist movies like Ocean's Eleven and The Italian Job, in which the first step is to find the right people for the team after which they can put together their "plan of attack".

The result is an exciting action movie, which looks amazing. Some sets are very impressive, especially when you know that they are set up in such a way that they can move and tilt. I will not go into further detail, but the result is stunning. It will definitely provide you with some "WOW!" moments, just like the first Matrix movie did a couple of years ago.

Before seeing this film I heard that it was a movie which was hard to understand, so I was preparing for something like Donnie Darko, which will make you think even more after you have finished watching it. I'll admit that you will have to keep focused, but I was impressed that such a complex story has been told in such an understandable way. Reason for this are the characters who explain a lot of things to each other and secondly the great editing, which will make sure you do not get lost in this complex maze.

There are a couple of reasons I decided to score it a 9.

After finishing the movie I did not get the feeling that I wanted to immediately see it again. I saw it last week and I still do not have that feeling. I do want to see it, but maybe in a couple of years. The reason I have this feeling is because the concept needs so much explanation that the first part spends a lot of time on it. When you watch the movie a second time, you will already know the rules. It's something I'm not looking forward to seeing again so soon.

The second reason is that I think not enough time was spent on the backgrounds of the main characters. The only person that you'll get to know more about is Cobb (Leonardo DiCaprio). His personal story is told in a lot of detail, but because the other characters only seem to be there to help him they felt as empty as the agents in the Matrix movies. They are used to tell the story without you knowing much about them. This made the movie feel very sterile to me, I missed a more personal touch which could have given the movie more "soul". So I didn't connect to the movie in the way I would have liked.

Despite these criticisms, Inception is an excellent movie. It offers amazing action scenes which you'll want to see again. The idea for the movie is unique and has been executed very well.

Christopher Nolan has managed to make another movie which you just can't afford to miss. It's not my personal movie of the year, this is still Mr.Nobody (which I've already seen twice) as I liked the more personal aspect of it. I can imagine that for a lot of people it will be though, as it's an impressive piece of film making.

9.title: Inception: The epitome of cinematic love
9.content:
Before going to Inception, I know this much about Nolan, I loved Batman Begins and Dark Knight and I didn't like Memento but I don't remember why - it may have been my state of mind, so I will rent it again to see what happened. I also knew I was excited about seeing Inception thanks to fantastic trailers and reviews.

Arriving at the local, usually "ok" Carmike theater, I was upset they put Inception on the smaller, non-digital screen. I hate you now, Carmike.

Leaving Inception, I was mostly fretting over the ending, not knowing what it was that happened. I will have to get back to figuring that out later. As for the rest of the movie, I can safely say I have never seen a solid, mature movie like this. As one wonders if we leave our brains at the door or bring it ready for action, don't concern yourself. There is absolutely something for all. Where thought seemingly is abandoned and action takes over, we all know what happens when bullets fly...or do we? Because of the varying levels of involvement, you have to analyze the action and the possible consequences of it. Believe me, consequences are always in the middle of the moment.

Visually, I do not see how anyone can be disappointed. I do believe the true adrenaline junkie will be disappointed, however. Despite the amount of action, Inception, to be so truly admired, requires much thought, and that's a much appreciated positive concept these days.

Personally, I am so thankful there are people like Nolan out there. He convinced me that he cares about his creations. Inception is probably one of the most completely respectable movies as far as I am concerned. Nothing lacked except for one thing - the explanation for the ending. I need more time to finish my thoughts on that. Everything else was great. Acting, action, visuals, the cute musical allusion to one of the best performers in Inception, the mystery, and the perplexing concept of the story itself all come together as the key to true cinematic success.

You might think I would give it a 10 but because of the stymieing end, I am going to be stubborn enough to give it a 9. Loved Inception and thanks again Mr Nolan!

9.title: A Original Blockbuster
9.content:
By Mindself

When it comes to studio blockbuster tent poles, this summer of films are filled with remakes, sequels, and adaptations of mediocre material. The public is itching for some sort of originality and volume, something to grasp and talk about in years to come. Almost ten years ago Christopher Nolan's Memento got critically acclaim for it's dark tale of obsession and themes of scarred memories. It also had a unique narrative mixed with a film noir style. After a decade of memorable films such as Insomnia and The Prestige, and the highly successful Batman film, The Dark Knight from two years ago, Christopher Nolan is now becoming a prosperous and renowned director in Hollywood. In my opinion he's one of the best directors in the past decade. In his latest effort, Inception, Christopher Nolan took those reoccurring themes of obsession and scarred memories and gave us again an unique narrative and style but this time he applied it with a summer blockbuster budget of $150 million (15x more than the budget of Memento) while satisfying the anxious moviegoers.

Inception is an unconventional heist film that's about an elite group of people, where each individual has their own unique ability, so they can go into a person's dream and extract whatever information or secrets that they may have and a give it to their client for their own self gain. It stars Leonardo DiCaprio, who plays the main protagonist Cobb, Joseph Gordon-Levitt as Cobb's assistant, Ken Watanabe as their client, Tom Hardy who also assist Cobb, and Ellen Page as the rookie in the group. All in which acted very well but most notable is Tom Hardy who played the badass Forger. What is also noticeable is the vast differences in the cast, whether that be race, gender, age, or their many years in Hollywood. Each actor or actress brought an amazing performance for a film, that at times, is difficult to comprehend.

Visually it's stunning and memorizing. Nolan knows how to cater to the crowd and he does it elegantly and unforced. His use of CG is unique because in some cases, he has the viewer fill in the blanks with their imagination. He doesn't take the effects for granted though. He also used practical effects, especially in a specific set piece that Joseph Gordon-Levitt was floating believably. His cinematographer, Wally Pfister, is also great. He didn't waste one frame and captured it's dark but at times hopeful scenery of several international locations wonderfully. I can't remember a film that attributes several locations and insert it as one of the plot devices. Nolan does it in every act of the film. Also the music by Hans Zimmer, who him and Pfister worked in most of Nolan's work, gave one of the highest energetic and at times suspenseful piece of composition of music this year. He also captured the mood and exhilaration of the film for each set piece with his music.

As for the flaws, couple of the characters accents did get in the way of the dialogue. Also there's a couple of questionable plot holes or arcs in the story that wasn't explained well enough to make sense. Nolan didn't hesitate in creating a mythology within the film. When he established the rules, he does it so fast and well, we question what's actually going on at times. The opening scene is the best example for this. No doubt there's a significant amount of exposition in the film. In which, you have to pay attention to every detail of the film, whether it's explaining what's a person's expertise is or setting the rules within a dream.

In all, if you're looking for a great time and want an intelligent but incredibly visualize blockbuster, then Inception is for you. Don't get it twisted though, not to over hype Nolan or the films credibility, it's a great film just don't expect it to make a whole lot of sense at times. Like I said, you have to pay attention to it's detail. Also he has all the intentions to set forth in making the summer blockbuster we all wanted, but it's disguised as being one of the most original and intriguing films this year. As you leave, not only will you asked yourself what just happen, you would like to watch it again in case something's missed.

check out artisticalliance.org for more impressions.

9.title: A film which doesn't underestimate the viewer
9.content:
As a film-goer, it feels great not to be underestimated. It doesn't happen very often, but you can trust Christopher Nolan not to do it once. Although I'm not someone who watches films because of their director, I was and will be willing to make an exception with Nolan - especially after Batman Begins and, more importantly, The Dark Knight. Inception had all the elements which enthralled me with Nolan's previous work: the enjoyably intricate plot, great pacing and faith in storytelling instead of special effects (although, in this case, the fantastic effects were there to support the narrative).

I love the fact that the film lacks stock characters, and that the focus of the film stays on the inception mission throughout the film instead of slipping to trite plot "twists" in order to draw audience. That is so hard to come by, and I always appreciate it. Inception doesn't offer easy solutions and let the viewer just sit there and take it all in.

The cast was, needless to say, superb. I was a bit prejudiced against DiCaprio as I had had enough of him already during the Titanic era, but in Inception, he was terrific, very intense. As for the female leads, Cotillard and Page, I have nothing but praise. They were not cast for their sex appeal, which I don't mean as an euphemism for unattractiveness - they were there for their powerful presence and credibility, which is, again, rare and goes to show that this film has more than just superficial potential. Funnily enough, a day before seeing Inception I watched the 90's teen comedy 10 Things I Hate About You, starring Joseph Gordon-Levitt. I'm so glad to see him back on screen in this great company.

I went to see this film with my father who's very rarely impressed by films not regarded as 'classics', and very refrained from praise. His first word after the Inception screening was 'breathtaking.' I was completely quiet on the way home, and by the time I got there, my thoughts raced with acclaim and I had already adopted the film to my Top 5 list and Nolan as one of my favorite directors. Inception is a film that you can't leave at the movie theater, because you know that you have just seen a future classic.

9.title: Nolan's new work is well dreamy...
9.content:
Firstly, let's get the bad stuff out of the way. Luckily it isn't a film related but more to do with the cinema. I saw this on a stupidly small screen that didn't justify a big film like this plus the cinema had terrible audio with the film's dialogue being at times barley audible, whilst much of the other sounds being crystal clear. This really hampered my enjoyment to some extent as I struggled to hear what was being said and it is a film that had a lot of explanation happening.

So the film, well it pretty amazing, it is a hyped up film that lives up to its hype. It looks incredible for a start, everything visually works, the settings, the styling and the special effects. The cast are all very good. Ellen Page is far the annoying Ellen Page we've seen before and Leonardo DiCaprio is really great in this, in fact I like him more and more as he gets older. The stand out performance for me is from Marion Cotillard who is not only stunning, she proves again that she is a fine actor. I'm yet to see her in anything that she hasn't been good. The films start is perhaps a little confusing-not helped by the lack of audio- but gradually it becomes more coherent. It is a truly original and exciting story, although similarity to other films can be made, this hold it's own absolutely.

The story is an exciting and gripping one and despite the long running time, it flows along brilliantly. The blending of reality and dreamworlds are executed perfectly and whilst the film relies on special effects, they are so dazzling that it barley registrars. There are some spectacular images, the streets of Paris folding over on itself is breathtaking and then there is the use of slow motion, when the street scape starts exploding in Paris or when the van falls towards the water and we see the sleeping occupants follow gravity. One of my favorite moments is during the later scenes where Arthur-played by Joseph Gordon-Levitt- in a seemingly weightless world runs around a rotating room and corridor and then ropes the bodies together placing them in a lift. I was so amazed by this, yet struggled with how it was done, it look like it was filmed in one of those planes that achieve weightlessness.

This is an all round impressive feature that shows that Christopher Nolan is a remarkable film maker. I think it's a film that deserves several viewings to fully appreciate and understand it, but one that is well worth it.

9.title: Great Play On The Mind!!!
9.content:
Inception: planting a thought into a person's sub – conscious without stealing the idea; which is exactly what writer/director Christopher Nolan did in his newest acclaimed box office action thriller since The Dark Knight. He set out to do exactly what he planned by planting thoughts of unimaginable ideas and theories into the audiences mind. "Applying a vivid sense of procedural detail to a fiendishly intricate yarn set in the labyrinth of the subconscious, the writer-director has devised a heist thriller for surrealists," as cited by Justin Chang from Variety Magazine.

Our guide in this in this high stakes sci-fi thriller and espionage is Dom Cobb (Leonardo Dicaprio) whose job title is "extractor" because of the way he is able to invade a person's mind and extract valuable information which in a black market of corporate intelligence worth a fortune. What is so thrilling about Dom Cobb is that the main antagonist in this story becomes his own subconscious which is haunted by his late wife Mal (Marion Cotillard), who has a nasty habit of showing up in his mind and wreaking havoc on his missions. The battle amongst himself presents a romantic drama aspect to the story when Cobb plants the idea that "love never dies in your mind, and that imagining a life with someone for 50 years subconsciously where your mind makes everything real and you never age and then waking up again and spending the rest of your life with someone" presents a beautiful idea of how far a person is willing to go to be with someone, however the irony is never understanding what is real and not real. This aspect of the story plays on human emotion which adds to the suspense of the story.

In classic heist-movie tradition, various specialists make up Cobb's team: Arthur (Joseph Gordon-Levitt) his longtime friend, Eames (Tom Hardy) a "forger" who can shape shift; Ariadne (Ellen Page) the "architect" who builds the labyrinth in the victim's mind that the team must perverse and Yusuf (Dileep Rao), who supplies the powerful sedative that pulls Fischer and Cobb's gang into a collective coma. The casting is very calculated and well put together giving the idea that each character pulls their weight bringing their personalities into play with the exception of Ariadne (Ellen Page) and her "Juno-esque" side commentary which becomes annoying in some parts and refreshingly comical in other scenes.

The visuals are amazing reminiscent of the matrix style scenes and fast paced camera cuts that leave you feeling a constant rush as if constantly in a dream. The plot is a constant ride moving at speeds that can sometimes seem hard to understand but Nolan keeps you interested constantly with constant ideas and theories that leaves you questioning if the ideas can in fact be real. In agreement with Peter Travers from Rolling Stone Magazine: "The visuals, shot by the gifted Wally Pfister on locations from the steaming heat of Morocco to the snow-capped Alps, are astounding. One segment, in which a freight train barrels through a traffic-clogged street, is jaw-dropping. Just as impressive is the way Nolan stays true to the rules of his own brain-teasing game." In conclusion the movie a total knockout bring to the screen an aspect of romance, drama, sci fi, and a thrilling ride that anyone whom enjoys a mental roller coaster through unknown theories would enjoy. Christopher Nolan once again does a great job by playing a game with people's minds and leaves you're wondering if everything in the movie is truly possible.

9.title: Brilliant.
9.content:
That word gets thrown around a lot - probably way too often, actually - when critics are trying to describe films they've particularly enjoyed, but halfway through "Inception," I realized there was really no other word to describe it. Even if you don't love the film (and it isn't quite flawless), purely on a conceptual level it's completely out there. This is one of those movies that comes along very rarely that assembles various film clichés, but spins them in such a new, fresh and exciting way that it feels like it's reinvented the wheel.

Like I said, it's certainly assembled from some basic stock clichés (Man Who Must Get Back His Kids, "Assemble Your Team," Dead Lover Whose Memory Haunts Hero, conceptual similarities to The Matrix and an action scene literally pulled right out of a James Bond movie, etc., etc., etc.,), the way Nolan pulls it all together is wholly unique. I have never seen a movie like this before. I was enthralled from beginning to end, and I totally understood why it took him ten years to finish this screenplay -- I mean, can you imagine keeping track of what's going on between all the various dream sequences? It'll be interesting to see what kind of goofs nerds with too much time on their hands pick out when it hits DVD.

Having said that, I feel it's short of perfect. For starters, Nolan still hasn't quite grasped the staging of an action sequence. He cuts around way too fast and you can't quite figure out what's going on. Sometimes it works -- I liked it in Batman Begins when he makes his first appearance and it's like an attack out of an alien movie because it's all edited incomprehensibly -- but I would have liked to get a better picture of that terrific fight Joseph Gordon-Levitt's character has during a particularly unique sequence. The way Nolan has edited this scene is so up-close and frantic that, even though it's still totally awesome, you kinda wish he'd pull back and let you get a clearer picture of the whole set and just watch it unfold. I felt the same way during the snowmobile chases and fight scenes -- just a bit too chaotic to keep up with. Sometimes it matches the frantic pace of the movie, but as with both Batman films (even though they were otherwise great movies), most of the time you get the feeling that he's just not comfortable with an action scene. He needs to get another editor who understands that element a bit better because he would otherwise be an almost limitless director.

Minor flaws that keep a 9/10 from being a 10/10. It's hard for me to knock Toy Story 3 down from my favourite film of '10, but for sheer originality this would win. It's definitely the second best film I've seen all year and, along with TS3, a standout from an otherwise dreary summer. Go see this if you've tired of brainless entertainments and welcome the idea of being able to talk about the film you've just seen on your way out of the theater instead of fishing for conversation starters.

When I saw the preview I thought they gave away the best special effect. I was wrong. There's a zero gravity fight scene which completely one-ups The Matrix (the original).

I'm not a big fan of DiCaprio, but he did a good job here. Everyone did a good job. The cast was excellent. This story is character driven. The special effects, although very excellently executed, are but a minor character in the grand role of things, which is how it should be (for how it shouldn't be, see second and third Matrix trilogy iterations, or the first three Star Wars episodes. Or better yet, don't).

Christopher Nolan just keeps getting better and better. Kudos to him. Batman Begins was excellent; the Dark Knight better still. I greatly appreciate Nolan's body of work.

I especially appreciated what I perceived to be the underlying message: let it go. Don't get bogged down by issues. Don't beat yourself up in an over-self-indulgent emotional orgy. Let things go and live here in the present. In the real world.

Yeah, I rarely give movies a nine (let alone a ten), but this movie is excellent. It was especially interesting to me that the score of the film was very similar to the music I normally have going in my head. Another movie like that is Ink which gets an eight.

Well done cast and crew for making a superlative experience. I rarely see movies multiple times in the theater, but I'm so totally going to go see this movie again, hopefully in Imax. And maybe again after that.

9.title: "Inception" is a modern masterpiece of sci-fi genre. Thanks to the complexity of its narrative, the film allows for multiple equally satisfying conclusions
9.content:
"Inception" does not seek to simplify its narrative for the viewer. Requiring the spectator's logical reasoning to the maximum, the film starts from an intelligent and complex premise, exploring the universe of dreams in a very logical and rational way, even though it opens spaces for oneiric and disconnected visions so common when we are dreaming, as when Cobb rubs between two walls trying to escape from pursuers (in a moment worthy of a nightmare) or when a train crosses a street full of cars - and the most interesting thing is that these visions always have some connection with the dreamers, as in this case where the train is a reflection of a striking phrase spoken by Cobb. Also intelligently, Nolan justifies these slightly confusing environments, which completely escape what we expect in a dreamlike environment, by using architects to design the dream world - Nash (Lukas Haas), at first, and then Ariadne. Even so, it is interesting to note how the real world directly interferes with dreams, as when Cobb falls into the bathtub while sleeping and, immediately, the water invades his dream, just as the rain in Yusuf's dream only reflects his desire to urinate ("Don't I could have urinated earlier!", complains Arthur).

Right away, Nolan inserts an important premise that makes the viewer get used to the complex idea of several layers of dreams, bringing Cobb and Saito back from two dreams to waking up on a train, which is essential for us to better understand the exceptional third. Act of "Inception". Staying true to the narrative's internal logic, Nolan also clearly and coherently explains some important concepts, such as the interesting concept of the difference in the passage of time in each dream level. But despite this narrative complexity, "Inception" never leaves the spectator confused, thanks to the clarity with which the director conducts the project, trusting the spectator's intelligence by avoiding the excess of information that could pollute the narrative.

With a large and very talented cast, Nolan also manages to extract great performances from practically everyone involved, even if they are in smaller roles, as in the case of Tom Berenger, who lives Uncle Browning, and Michael Caine as the teacher. Living the projection of wife Mal, Marion Cotillard convinces in the role and even manages to plant doubt in Cobb's head (and the viewer) at a certain moment, just as Ken Watanabe conveys confidence in the skin of businessman Saito. And if Cillian Murphy appears correctly weakened as the indecisive Fischer, Joseph Gordon-Levitt makes his Arthur a captivating character, especially when he needs to take the reins at a certain moment at the risk of putting all the team's action in jeopardy - and he does it a lot good.

We also have Tom Hardy, who lives the chameleon Eames and has a fundamental role in several moments (it is worth noting the subtlety with which he "transforms" into Uncle Browning and vice versa, especially when he is sitting on the rocks after emerging from the water in the dream of Yusuf), as well as Ellen Page's architect Ariadne (the eternal Juno!), who works as a kind of guide for the viewer, with her questions bringing up vital explanations for us to understand what is happening on the screen, but who also collaborates a lot with the team during the mission. But the highlight of "Inception" is even star Leonardo DiCaprio, who confirms his talent and charisma by carrying this complex project with ease. Wishing only to be able to return home and see his children again, his Cobb moves in his struggle to forget Mal, put in check every time he enters a dream, involuntarily projecting his "dead" wife and putting his missions at risk, in a reflex straight from her traumatic death which DiCaprio demonstrates so well. Precisely conveying Cobb's dilemma when his convictions are questioned by his wife, the actor makes the viewer share his feelings, further demonstrating the character's growing anguish convincingly throughout the narrative.

Showing perfect framing and symmetrical planes, in addition to beautiful camera movements such as the tracking that reveals the structure of the limbo, Christopher Nolan pays attention to the visual aspect, also using slow motion with precision in crucial moments, such as when objects begin to explode in Paris after Cobb reveal that Ariadne is in a dream, in a moment that also confirms the quality of the visual effects of "Inception". And what about the strange and magnificent moment when the city bends and brings the roofs of buildings together? In addition, Nolan also shows competence in directing the action scenes, such as the chases, the shootings and the invasion of the fortress, but always inserting these sequences in an organic way and contributing to the progress of the narrative, proving his ability to command blockbusters with brain, already revealed before in the excellent "Batman Begins" and "The Dark Knight". Obviously, he has a talented technical team to achieve this visual perfection. Note, for example, the difference between tones in Wally Pfister's photography, which helps to clearly identify which dreams the characters are in, in addition to revealing important characteristics of each dreamer.

The spectacular visual effects mentioned above make everything more convincing and realistic, also standing out in the fight that takes place in Arthur's dream, in which the characters float on the screen due to the alteration of gravity, in an interesting reflection of what happens in the chaotic environment in which they are dreaming in the previous layer. Also noteworthy are the great sound effects and sound design, which capture every movement of the characters, the shots, the noise of cars and even the crack of a broken glass, vital at a certain point in the narrative. Hans Zimmer's soundtrack draws little attention to itself, appearing only in specific moments and gaining strength in the big scenes, especially through Edith Piaf's diegetic music that connects dreams - which also makes a reference to the Oscar-winning role of Marion Cotillard. Closing the technical part, Lee Smith's exceptional montage maintains a dynamic rhythm throughout the narrative, reaching almost perfection during the four simultaneous dreams (which we will discuss in a moment) by moving between each one of them in a fluid and organic way.

After strictly complying with the plan, the agents finally manage to invade Fischer's mind, starting the sensational sequence in which, they invade dreams within dreams, even going through three layers until the young businessman is reached in the last stage, putting him at risk. The whole mission. That's when they decide to save Fischer and look for Saito, also injured and already abandoned in limbo, going to a fourth layer and creating an interesting challenge for the spectator, now forced to follow four parallel actions, at different time levels and with different objectives. Nolan conducts the entire sequence with mastery and reaches technical perfection in what is certainly the great moment of "Inception", when the "kick" begins to bring the dreamers back to reality - and it is impressive how he respects with almost military rigidity the internal logic of the narrative, not just in this moment, but throughout the entire film. Relying again on the great work of editor Lee Smith, Nolan creates a beautiful and potentially tense sequence, capable of making us stick to the screen as we follow the characters awakening successively. Slow motion showing the van crash in the first dream, the elevator crash in the second, the fortress explosion that follows the moment Fischer opens the safe in the third, and the instant Ariadne throws Fischer off the building and into the fourth. Dream are memorable sequences, conducted at a perfect pace by Nolan, who still ties the narrative perfectly by bringing Cobb waking up on Limbo beach again, as well as in the foreground of the feature.

As if that weren't enough, we still have the beautiful ending, with everyone waking up on the plane and Cobb confirming that his mission was successful when he saw Saito picking up the phone, allowing him to go through immigration and meet his children again. And so Nolan decides to play with our perception by ending this masterpiece of science fiction with a controversial shot, in which we see the totem turning, but we do not see its fall, creating two interesting possibilities for interpretation. In the first and most plausible of them, Cobb returns home, finds his children in "real life" and the totem falls after the film ends. But the fact of cutting the shot before showing the object's fall raises another curious possibility, aired a few times during the narrative (especially by Mal and by a gentleman who administers sedation). Was Cobb living a long, complex dream? The fact that he is pursued by enemies and even authorities, just as the "dreamers" are pursued in the dreams he invades, reinforces this theory - and Nolan is smart enough not to show the fall of the totem, thus planting doubt in him. Our minds, especially since Mal asserts with conviction at several points that Cobb is the one who got trapped in the dream world, not her. And in this way, the director makes the viewer share the same doubt as the character, who, in the face of everything he has witnessed and experienced, no longer knows what a dream is and what is reality. Isn't it great?

Whether or not Cobb was dreaming is of little concern. Thanks to the complexity of its narrative, the film allows for multiple equally satisfying conclusions. And the best part is that, in order to completely decipher these alternatives, all the spectator has to do is give himself the gift of diving back into the intelligent and fascinating universe built by this man who has been confirming himself as one of the best directors of our time. A dream job, let's face it.

9.title: Inception Blast

Too much complicated movie. But can't be possible without Leo.., He is the perfect actor for movies like this.

In the first level, the team enter Yusuf's dream of a rainy Los Angeles. The team abducts Fischer, but it emerges that Fischer has been trained to resist extraction. He reflexively creates a team of bodyguards who protect him, wounding Saito severely. Even worse, a barreling freight train plows down the avenue, batting aside cars and trucks and cutting off Cobb, Yusuf and Ariadne from the rest of the team. Eames temporarily takes the appearance of Fischer's godfather, Peter Browning (Tom Berenger), to suggest Fischer reconsider his father's will. Yusuf drives the team in a van as the rest are sedated into the second level, a hotel dreamed by Arthur.

On this level, the extractors recruit Fischer, convincing him that his kidnapping was orchestrated by Browning and that they are Fischer's subconscious protectors. They persuade him to go down another level to explore Browning's subconscious (whereas it is actually a ruse to enter his own). The third level is a snowy mountain fortress dreamed by Eames. Meanwhile, Yusuf, under assault in the first level, accidentally initiates his kick too soon by driving off a bridge, removing the gravity of Arthur's dream world and causing an avalanche in Eames' dream. Arthur is forced to improvise a new kick using an elevator that will be synchronized with the van hitting the water, while the team in Eames' dream races to finish the job before the new round of kicks. Saito succumbs to his wounds, and Cobb's projection of Mal sabotages the plan by killing Fischer, sending them both into Limbo. Cobb and Ariadne enter Limbo to find Fischer and Saito, while Eames remains on his dream level to set up a kick by rigging the fortress with explosives. Cobb reveals to Ariadne that he and Mal went to Limbo while experimenting with the dream-sharing technology, where they spent "fifty years" of experienced time constructing a world from their shared memories while seemingly growing old together. Cobb confesses that in order to ensure Mal would leave Limbo, he had implanted the idea her reality was false in her head in the first place; this was how he knew that inception was possible. The experience destabilize Mal,and left her convinced that she was still dreaming. In an attempt to'wake up', Mal committed suicide, and tried desperately to persuadeCobb to do so too by incriminating him in her death. Facing a murdercharge, Cobb fled the U.S. His children, who appear frequently in hisdreams, are inCalifornia in the care of Professor Miles, who is Mal'sfather.

9.title: Inception's Unforgettable Twist
9.content:
Inception doesn't just tell a story; it weaves a labyrinth of intrigue and wonder. When I first witnessed its narrative acrobatics, I was left in awe, unable to share details for fear of spoilers. Suffice it to say, the movie poses questions that echo long after the credits roll.

The pivotal moment, that exchange between Cobb and Mal, is the linchpin of the entire tale. It's the cipher that unravels the enigma, offering a singular line that answers a multitude of queries. This is where the brilliance of Inception lies - in its ability to distill complexity into a single, impeccably crafted sentence.

Such cinematic finesse is a rare gift. Few films possess the dexterity to construct a tale so intricate, where viewers are held in suspense, eagerly awaiting that illuminating line. Yet, many fall short. They attempt the tightrope walk of complexity, but stumble and falter.

But Inception doesn't merely excel in its narrative. The cast, a constellation of talent, delivers performances that are nothing short of extraordinary. Each character is brought to life with a depth that leaves an indelible mark.

Wally Pfister's cinematography is a masterclass in visual storytelling. It paints the narrative with hues of awe and wonder, earning the accolades it rightly deserves. Hans Zimmer's original score, a symphony of brilliance, punctuates every beat with precision, heightening the cinematic experience to a crescendo of emotion.

And let's not forget the visual effects, a tapestry of imagination that dances on the screen. They're not just effects; they're an integral part of the narrative, pushing the boundaries of what we think is possible.

Inception isn't just a movie; it's a cinematic triumph, an opus of storytelling and technical mastery. It invites us to venture beyond the realms of reality, into a world where dreams and reality blur. It's an experience that transcends the screen, leaving an indelible mark on those fortunate enough to witness its magic.

9.title: An Incredible Sci-FI

I had heard previous comments on this film to be mind blowing and one of the best films of all time, and it was honestly fantastic, I really enjoyed it. The beginning of this film was chaotic and was a form of 'in media res', which is a technique to open a film which effectively throws the audience into the opening of a film that is full of action and chaos. I was confused, and invested in the action, having a certain desire to understand the situation, which proves the efficiency of this technique. The concept for this film, as itself, was already engrossing and intriguing, forcing the audience to, for a split second, question the reality of their dreams or materiality of their real life.

The editing of this film is something I definitely have to highlight in this film, it was perfect. The editing used in this film was subtle and unnoticed, which is what editing should be for a film, pure escapism for the audience rather than distracting them from the story. It raised tension as the characters were completing their mission, fast paced editing, as well as maintained the storyline so the audience can understand the scale and idea of the time frames in each person's dream they had infiltrated. The cinematography in this film was creative and visually interesting for the audience, showing the stakes and magnitude of a situation or subject.

The story seemed complex however not overly complex to the point where it seems unnecessary or just confusing by the end. I really appreciated the creativity in the concept of each dream affecting the subsequent dream, for example when the van in Robert Fischer's dream was flipping and Joseph Gordon-Levitt's character, Arthur, was fighting in a hotel and it began to rotate. I believe that this idea was great to begin with but was also executed practically with elegance and seamless fitting in the scene.

9.title: Inceptionally Brilliant in Every Way!
9.content:
'Inception' is a film which epitomises why I admire Christopher Nolan as a director so much, a remarkable phenomenon which is one of the 21st century's greatest sci-fi thrillers.

In a movie of this particular genre, I want the director/producer to stimulate my brain and keep me engaged with the viewing material. The classic movies are anchored by the cast and characters with strong personalities which don't render cardboard cut outs. Also, landscapes, expertly crafted usage of cinematography and choreography adds to the main aspects you should be searching for in a film which is worthy of being dubbed superb. With 'Inception', Nolan ticks all the boxes - and with sufficient ease, in a movie which exceeds all of his previous work.

It was due to the scarily good reception of superhero flick 'The Dark Knight' that Warner Brothers concealed their faith in Nolan by allowing him the opportunity to produce his long anticipated script. By hauling in the likes of Leonardo DiCaprio, Cillian Murphy, Ken Watanabe and Tom Hardy, it was clear Nolan had assembled an incredibly talented casting list; it's suffice to say that their portrayals of complexly detailed characters were nothing short of outstanding.

The synopsis is that a professional thief (DiCaprio), who can enter the minds of others and steal their most enclosed secrets, is forced on the run when he fails his assignment and his shady organisation intend to murder him. However, former enemy Saito (Watanabe) offers him a chance to eradicate his tarnished relationship with his former employers by offering him one final 'mind heist' assignment: Inception, the idea you must enter four dream state world's and plant an idea inside someone else's head instead of stealing it. DiCaprio is then forced to equip himself with an experienced set of individuals in order to complete this seemingly impossible task.

Not giving too much away, 'Inception' is without doubt one of the best films in its genre, and possibly the best of Nolan's career to date.

Beyond its technical brilliance, "Inception" delves into profound themes that resonate on both intellectual and emotional levels. The film invites audiences to reflect on the fragility of memory, the consequences of our actions, and the pursuit of redemption. Amidst the grand scale of its concept, "Inception" maintains a strong emotional core, grounding the story in relatable human experiences and creating a deeply affecting cinematic journey.

The meticulous sound design in "Inception" plays a crucial role in enhancing the film's immersive quality. The use of layered audio cues and hauntingly atmospheric soundscapes serves to heighten tension, create a sense of urgency, and emphasize the fluidity between dream levels. Hans Zimmer's iconic score, with its pulsating rhythms and haunting melodies, becomes an integral part of the film's fabric, driving the narrative forward and intensifying the emotional impact of key moments.

"Inception" solidifies its status as an exceptional film that seamlessly blends intricate storytelling, groundbreaking visuals, and profound themes. "Inception" is not just a film to be watched; it is an experience to be savored, contemplated, and discussed. 9.title: Dreams on top of dreams inside dreams
9.content: Setting the mind ablaze with inspired dream imagery, thought-provoking notions about reality, action sequences that leave the jaw dangling in wonder, and an emotional undercurrent to tie everything together, Christopher Nolan's Inception is a masterpiece. Though Nolan, who took ten years to write his screenplay, kept his production hush-hush, and the film's advertisements reveal little about the plot, the diminutive amount of pre-release information available has left audiences bewildered but intrigued. In the broadest of terms, the film is a heist-like science-fiction tale set in the open playground of dreams, where the rules of reality are controlled by a dreamer. But Nolan avoids falling into surrealist Dali territory, in that the dreamscapes serve as a carefully controlled environment with which to access the subconscious mind. The dream world comes with its own set of rules, which the audience learns in the film's first half in as much detail as possible. Cobb engages in a rare form of robbery when he enters the minds of his targets to extract ideas from their subconscious, all without the targets ever knowing. The success of every job depends on how well Cobb can control the dream and manipulate his mark into believing the dream is real. If the target becomes aware of the deception, that they are in truth inside a dream, the dream world falls apart and Cobb wakes up with nothing. But in order to successfully complete such a mission, the idea has to be implanted deep into the recesses of the subconscious, where the idea will grow naturally and the mark will never know the idea was not their own. To accomplish the seemingly impossible task of inception, Cobb assembles a team of skilled dream manipulators, all played by actors of the highest caliber. Together they prepare, walking the audience through the maze-like plan that finds intricate ways to implant the idea into the subconscious of their assigned mark, a young industrialist played by Cillian Murphy. Joseph Gordon-Levitt plays Arthur, Cobb's partner and expert in the dream world's rules. Dileep Rao's character Yusuf is a chemist who specializes in the drugs that keep Cobb's team sedated for the dream. A virtuoso display of action and ideas, the extended sequence involves layers of subterfuge that take place in a dream-within-a-dream-within-a-dream. But despite their likenesses to other material, Nolan lends his personal touch to each scene, allowing his story's environment and the way they are coordinated to leave us wowed by their originality. And, as the three sequences unfold, the audience is always aware of the overlaying stakes, and how everything going down onscreen relates to Cobb's emotional conflict. The altitudes may go even deeper than we realize in this sequence, but that's for the viewer to discover. Indeed, the finale plays out much in the order of David Cronenberg's eXistenZ, as the characters question the veracity of this or that reality. Since Memento, Nolan has always been interested in the mind's ability to create realities for and deceive itself. It's a theme that follows through Insomnia and The Prestige, and remains a crucial character trait for Bruce Wayne in the director's Batman films. Along with his complex narrative, which is divided between reality and several dream realities splitting off from one another, it becomes evident that many of the themes from Nolan's early work converge here into an impressive whole. The film has a way of using every method at its disposal, from settings realized through special effects to natural locations, to give the audience the impression that we are areally there,' because believing that becomes a crucial part of the story as the characters fall dangerously deeper into their dream state. As much as we are immersed in this experience visually and emotionally, composer Hans Zimmer's score plays a vital role in bringing these characters and the various realities together. His persistent music keeps an ever-present tempo, akin to The Dark Knight's score, and penetrates the viewer with deep horns that seem to blast straight through, reverberating with the audience straight to the bone. Zimmer's haunting music transcends the layers of the plot and offers an aural connective tissue for the production. So perhaps it's best to leave a comprehensive analysis for another time and simply say this is a perfect film, Nolan's highest masterpiece in a career teeming with little else except other masterpieces and, at the very least, other great films. How rare that a blockbuster of this size results in a thinking person's experience, filled with emotions and imagination, while also appealing to the more elementary need for thrills. This is the type of big-budget summer entertainment that could have easily reduced itself to a mere action movie, but Nolan makes Inception so much more by involving us in the fates of his fascinating characters and forcing his audience's participation on intellectual and awe-inspiring levels. When its breezy two-and-a-half hour runtime has elapsed, the audience is left to marvel over Nolan's production, completely ready to watch the film again as soon as possible and revel in its expert orchestration of ideas and action. It's one of the best films in recent years, and in an underwhelming year at the cinema, it's something truly extraordinary.

This is a real review. The 10 isn't me being funny; this is my system: any movie can be a 10 if it is GREATER THAN THE SUM OF ITS PARTS, however I see/ deem fit per each individual movie, in no comparison to other movies, except to help make a better judgment in terms of relativity and consistency in my rating system.

That being said, it gets a 10, because:

1) great casting, big and small, right choices were made, though not necessarily irreplaceable.

2) great performances by cast, with Leo leading the show like the master he is, though not particularly the best performance of his life he's just great all the time he chooses to work. Great support no doubt, each actor has continued on careers of their own lead roles.

3) high budget means it didn't need to cut corners to make the movie happen, so like all the crazy gravity defying scenes, environments, action scenes, top quality script, top notch cast only money can buy.

4) cinematography, top, shots look great, masterful, specially the water shots just stick to me like they're my own life memories.

5) script/ plot, innovative and clean to the point. Lengthy movie that is pretty much a thrilling ride the whole time. Though it concerns the whole entering dreams Sci fi aspect, it feels like a thriller in general, so even though it satisfies the science fiction genre, it does not count out audiences that are not fans of science fiction, like my mother for example, though the dream stuff does go over her head. Story/ movie could have gone many different ways, but overall good decisions were made for progressing and concluding the plot.

6) open ended resolution but that can be debated, in terms of getting closure for our protagonist and what his future holds.

7) it's a movie worth rewatching which I think is probably the most fundamental and consistent trait of a perfect movie, which leads to the next point.

8) timeless, I do believe this movie will stand the test of time because of its unique plot and quality and minimalist of any cgi used.

Finally, this could definitely be a 9, or an 8, or maybe even a 7 to some people... but realistically i don't think anyone on earth would or should give this movie less than that, because work and passion went into this movie; there is no way around that, and I happen to be one of the critics who appreciated all of it.

9.title: Brilliant!
9.content:
Christopher Nolan's execution of the Caped Crusader in the Dark Knight has exceeded every movie lover's expectations when it comes to cinema.

If you know nothing about Inception, at least know this: it is not a hoax. It is ingenious. Profoundly filled with knotty story lines, entirely problematic and mind manipulating to the t. Once this film takes foundation in your mind, it is merely impossible to eradicate.

Nolan's new movie is a colossal digital artefact and moulded in crafty puzzles rather than profound mysteries which only amplifies the intention of half the films thrill consisting of simply keeping up with it!

The big idea here is dream invasion. At some stage in the distant future, the technology of industrial espionage allows snoopers to infiltrate the dreams of CEOs to pinch commercially sensitive information.

Leonardo DiCaprio is Dom Cobb, is a skilled thief and is portrayed as the absolute best in the dangerous art of "extraction". However, DiCaprio's character holds a rare ability that has made him a desirable player in the perfidious new world of corporate espionage, though it has also made him an international fugitive, which consequently-and - in a rather way- has cost him everything he ever loved. Look at it as his final chance at redemption. All he needed do is accomplish the impossible inception. Instead of the perfect heist, Cobb and his team of specialists, co-starring Joseph Gordon-Levitt, Tom Hardy, Ellen Page and Ken Watanabe-have to pull the reverse. Their task is not to steal an idea, but to plant one. Japanese plutocrat Saito (Ken Watanabe) needs Cobb to infiltrate the mind of precarious young business man Robert Fischer Jr. (Cillian Murphy) and infuse in him an idea of his own accord in aid to break up the family empire that is hurting Saito's profits. They plan to drug Fischer on a 10-hour plane journey whereby they will create a triple-decker dream. That is a dream-within-a-dream-within-a-dream. A littler Bermuda triangle-esq., nonetheless, a hell of an experience.

Mind all the haziness that is being received throughout a vast majority of the film because it is far from a movie to be analysed, more that of to be mused over; landscapes that reach vertical ends, buildings that manoeuvre like pulsing three-dimensional maps that are part of a pop-up book in arrears or mirrors that crunch by touch and transfigure into long inter-twined bridges. Inception has provided us with a chance to marvel at the vivacity of filmmaker who probes you to emotionally invest in avowed mental constructs - and does not fail to succeed.

Disregarding all elements of art the film proudly carries with it, at hand is much, much more. A story line which is tantalizingly performed by endowed, graceful actors. Inception punches in with possibly the most ambiguous opening scene since DiCaprio's prior film 'Shutter Island'. Which beckons the question are we to suppose a pattern will emerge with future work? We are introduced to a gathered-up-in-the-beach-waves Dom Cobb - which pleasantly triggers some 'Titanic' reminiscences as he is seen panicking from impacting water.

Throughout the entire motion picture DiCaprio staggeringly delivers a gifted, accomplished performance. The genuine emotion of his character shines through at unbelievable height with such ease. His work continues to fascinate me. DiCaprio is in full charge of himself in Inception, not an easy job seeing as much of it is special effects driven, but you can always rely on the fact that you can lean into DiCaprio and appreciate the emotion.

With Inception, Christopher Nolan has effectively proved that summer blockbusters can be compelling as they can be intelligent. My single given advice to any of you who may find yourselves dwelling in this magical IMAX can be no more than do not linger for a 'ta-dah' and 'it was all a dream' moment. It will only hinder your enjoyment and waste your time.

9.title: Sci-fi perfection
9.content:
Inception is truly one of a kind. A concept which has long gestated in Christopher Nolan's mind, his eye for drama mixed with his large scale sensibilities ring true in Blockbuster season making Inception a true original in the sea of reboots, remakes and sequels.

To try and explain Inceptions many plot twists and incredibly intelligent arcs, would be a foolish task. As Nolan himself has been reluctant to. The best way to approach the film would be with an open mind, if you are prepared to be taken on a ride of a lifetime, then trust that you 100% will. If Avatar was a seminal film in technology (although coming out as a rather poor film, in my opinion), then Inception is seminal in it's storytelling. With a 148 minute running time, you would expect a lot to take place, but what you wouldn't expect is the pace of it all. I did not think at one time in the film about how long was left. I was simply blown away by the depth in every single part of the film. If my enthusiasm for the storytelling aspect of the film has left you worried about the spectacle, then don't worry. They are, as hinted in the trailer, incredible, looking real and unbelievable simultaneously. The most pleasing thing about the action set pieces, is that they are genuinely used to illustrate the story, rather than to blow stuff up a la Michael Bay.

With this complex movie in it's high concept, a stellar cast is needed. And Nolan as always, delivers with just that. This is vintage DiCaprio, perhaps only equalled in The Aviator, which is even more impressive as his role as Cobb in Inception is not a showy one, needing DiCaprio to be the constant at the centre of the film. And he pulls off Cobb's emotional contradictions sublimely. The rest of the cast members all shine in parts of the films, Cillian Murphy shows off his usually non-existent tender side, Gordon-Levitt bottles his usual charm for his confidently reserved turn as the reliable Arthur, Watanabe is devilish as the seemingly ambiguous Saito, Page shows why she's the next big female star and Tom Hardy revels in being the comic relief of the film compared to his recent turns as decidedly psychopathic characters.

Overall, Nolan has indeed surpassed himself. He has created a world as expansive as his Gotham, a plot dwarfing the intricacies of Memento and one which blows The Prestige's cinematic reveal out of the water. This is truly unmissable cinema. Revel in it, we've still got to wait a whole two years before Batman 3.

9.title: Great movie
9.content: Christopher Nolan's latest venture, Inception, is everything Hollywood needs: human story, cool special effects, and an original idea. The movie works on so many levels it cannot help but be entertaining. Cobb (Leonardo DeCaprio) is a thief. However, he does not steal jewelry, bonds, money or cars, but ideas. He does this by visiting the dream scape of his victims. It has to be done in a clever way because some people are aware of this type of crime. Not only are there natural defenses in our dreams, but trained ones as well. His team is made an offer, though. The offer comes from Sato (Ken Watanabe) who wishes to do the opposite: he wants to plant an idea in a rival competitor, played by Cillian Murphy. Now Cobb's team must invade Murphy's dream. The movie works on so many levels. In the first place, we must learn the rules. For example, someone entering a dream cannot draw attention to themselves or alter the dream from their psyche or the dreamer will catch on. The dreamer also has "memories" that act as defenses, much like White Blood Cells that fight infections. Also, five minutes in real time equals something like an hour in dream time. You can invade a dream on two levels, or have a dream within a dream. The invaders must keep some sort of physical device and hold it to memory within the dream to make sure they are dreaming. Then there is the story of relationships gone awry. In fact, we learn the dreams are ways of dealing with past traumas. Cobb must learn to deal with his own baggage. This relates to the death of his wife and the alienation from his children. Unfortunately, they manifest themselves when he tries to invade the dream of others. What I truly like about this film was the metaphysical questions that deal with guilt, love, loss, and fear. What makes all these things work so well is the even-handed direction and screenplay of Nolan that keeps our interest piqued, but at the same time does not reveal everything. It also has a very dark element without being cynical or depressing. Instead, there is redemption. Nolan keeps getting better without falling backwards like M. Night Shymalan has done over the last half-decade. This is equally true in his writing as well as his directing. He is truly the best director out there at this time.
