9.title: "An idea is like a virus": Committing the perfect crime
9.content: "An idea is like a virus. Resilient. Highly contagious. And even the smallest seed of an idea can grow. It can grow to define or destroy you." Dominick Cobb, (played by Leonardo DiCaprio). Inception was a film directed and written by Christopher Nolan and released as a blockbuster in the summer of 2010 Inception is an invasion and extraction of the deepest secrets within a dream and eventually a place for a seed of an idea. Cobb the protagonist and master of incepting dreams was hired to assemble a team and plant an idea into an heir of a major corporation's mind, which proved even more difficult than imaginable. Although, some will say that the concept of Inception is too complicated and all over the place, everyone should watch this movie because it's an intense, thought-provoking thriller that will keep you wondering even after the credits begin to roll. Inception can be seen as a complex and chaotic film due to the overwhelming visuals that blend seamlessly together from the dream state and reality the characters flow between. It begins with the introduction of Dominick Cobb who is the best "extractor" in the game, Saito, who is eventually known as the "Tourist," and Arthur the "Point Man." The encounter of these three men meeting leads to an opportunity for Cobbs to finally be able go home but first he must face his own nightmares. Dreaming allows us to create our own worlds and alternate realities, but what if someone could control the dream and extract important information that no one should know. Now what if an idea can be planted that could cause a life changing moment. Eventually, the idea that was planted could be traced to where it originated from. So how could this job be accomplished without it being sourced? Cobb recruits Ariadne, she is their "Architect" who is in charge of designing the mazes within the dream to keep the subject lost and the team in control. Cobb then pursues Eames, the charismatic "Forger" whose job is to study mannerism and chrematistics so he can impersonate someone important to the person being incepted. Cobbs has almost everyone he needs, but the last piece he needs is Yusuf the "Chemist. Yusuf created the drug so powerful that it can sedate everyone to be able to share dreams for a long period of time. The perfect team to help create the perfect crime without it ever being able to be traced. Cobb has a great team, but the real question is is it enough to get the job done. They are not only up against the challenge of planting an idea that would be undetectable, but the team is in a race against time, while Cobb is fighting against his conscience that is haunting him and making the mission almost impossible to achieve. Even when you think he's made it out, the fact that the movie has been going back between the idea of dreams and reality you are met with the thought of, "was any of it real?" Did he make it out or was it all a dream while his reality sits somewhere else? Inception is a film that keeps you drawn in between the jumps between reality and dreams. Its complex plot hinders the ability to decipher who is the enemy or the concept of what is reality. Through-out Inception idea of who is really in control begins to rise and creates an uneasy feeling of doubt. The feeling of a life-or-death timer brings a level of intensity to the brink of mutual annihilation. Inception has action, romances and wonder, it has the ability to alter the way reality is viewed.

9.title: INCEPTION!!An Outstanding Package Of fiction and action With Some Unignorable flaws??
9.content:
Inception is not a complicated movie; it is merely a different movie. No one has ever made a movie about dream levels where a heist crew goes into someone's mind to implant an idea.Here its to be noted,the movie is named INCEPTION because its all about incepting/implanting ideas in someones mind to make him/her work to implement a specific purpose.

1.Firstly i would like to mention here christopher nolan worked 10 years in this script and now i understand why??its a damn outstanding masterpiece i have ever seen.Secondly casting choices took this movie to another level. 2.leonardo as always lived the character and rocked on it 3.Tom Hardy was also quiet well,he worked as much as he possibly could in his screen time. 4.Ellen Page,i must say,was the perfect choice for an young clever architect,who as well stole the spotlight for her charm and beauty. 5.Marion,oh my god!!!!!her expressions were enough to convince the audiences the depth and importance of her character ,though she had the shortest screen time here.Still she drew half of my attractions towards her,i was really waiting in the whole movie thinking when she is gonna jump and spoil cobbs plan. 6.Lastly,to me it was Cillian Murphy who was probably in the second lead here,because the whole plot evolves around him.And frankly,he had done his job well.

















SPOILER AHEAD!!!!

So a large portion of the film is given over to explanations, but Inception does not need to be solved even with its ambiguous ending. Nolan patiently walks his audience through the mechanics of dreams and the trauma of his protagonist, Cobb (Leonardo DiCaprio).When i look at all the contours of the movie and how it unfolds, Inception is far more concerned with how dreams-lies we tell ourselves-shape us rather than reality. While the conflict between reality/dreams may haunt Cobb(decaprio) and his relationship with Mal (Marion Cotillard), it doesn't drive the plot forward. What drives Cobb is the mission to perform inception on Fischer (Cillian Murphy), which in turn gives Cobb the drive to get home to his family. To create dreams for another and create inspiration is what allows Cobbs to reach his aspiration-reunification with his children. While Cobb wrestles with the nature of his reality (hence the frequent spinning of the top), Mal's fate becomes more of a cautionary tale and yet one he can't fully escape. The trauma has become his reality, and we see that dreams are no escape as she haunts Cobb wherever he goes.The only way to work through this trauma is through a shared dream, which is where Inception basically functions like a movie about movies. Cobb is the director, Arthur (Joseph Gordon-Levitt) is the producer, Ariadne (Ellen Page) is the writer, Eames (Tom Hardy) is the actor, Saito (Ken Watanabe) is the studio, and Fischer is the audience (Yusuf's (Dileep Rao) role is a bit more nebulous, but he represents the work of the craftspeople to make the dream possible even if it's not glamorous or easy to describe). For Nolan and Inception, lies are what we tell each other and tell ourselves to move forward. Nolan is a firm believer that a lie can tell the truth when it's presented at the right angle. Fischer needs catharsis from his father's death. It's a lie that his father wanted him to break up the company and wanted him to be his own man, but it doesn't matter, because that's what Fischer needs to move forward. It may not be his idea, and arguably he's been manipulated in a fairly grotesque fashion by having his mind hijacked, but the lie brings him peace. This in turn foreshadows what will happen with Cobb.

9.title: A solid sci-fi action from Nolan
9.content:
Dreams and reality, being awake and dreaming. In a sense both states are just as real, when you experience them, but dreams are more fickle, as even they seem real at the time, the moment we awake those memories which just moments ago were so vivid, crumble into nonsensical images, that escape your thoughts at the moment you are fully awake. But still, you can remember those images and dreams. They linger behind your subconscious and can jump out suddenly. They can be a seed for an idea.

That is something Christopher Nolan explores with his masterfully directed Inception. True enough, I don't think it's his best movie to date, but it is well made in all aspects. The cast is solid and the script has very few weaknesses in it. But still there was something in it, which I can't yet put my finger on, that just didn't clicked with me.

Saito (Ken Watanabe) hires Cobb (Leanardo DiCaprio) to insert an idea to the mind of his competitor (Cillian Murphy). This is done by entering the subjects dreams and trying to make the subject believe, that the idea comes from him and no one else. This is a good premises for a movie, that happens in a multiple levels of human consciousness, such providing a playground for spectacular action and visuals.

Entering some ones dreams isn't easy. To do that, they need an architect, Ariadne (Ellen Page), to construct a dream world so real, that the subject doesn't suspect a thing. Other players in the dream are Cobbs ensemble of trusted men, such as Arthur (Joseph Gordon-Levitt) and Eams (Tom Hardy), who from their part try to keep the subjects defenses occupied.

All in all, Inception is one of the best movies this summer, there's no weak link among the cast and the movie rolls on like a steam train. Nolan has managed to direct an ambitious Hollywood movie, which is full of originality. By itself the feat is remarkable, though not quite a home run.

9.title: An excellent and effective movie, but not absolutely perfect
9.content:
Inception is a movie based on an Excellent idea that, if put on the wrong hands - that is, anyone but Nolan and maybe Pixar - would be ruined. This is not the case here: a brilliant, well constructed thriller that, although being quite simple, is of a VERY complex nature. Nolan could have spent more time explaining the structure of this universe, but he leaves the story to explain it - only using a couple of scenes between DiCaprio and Ellen Page to explain what could not be explained outside the movie's plot. Truly a movie that will be kept in your mind for a long time, and praised as one of the best ever conceived - a mix between the intelligence of Memento, the tension of men-on-the-job thrillers like Ronin or Munich, and the dreamlike environment of Eternal Sunshine of the Spotless Mind.

This movie, however, it's not without flaws. Ellen Page, as ever, "sinks" the movie with her sub par acting and her "teenage" acting stance, in a role that should require something better or more mature.

(Di Caprio is competent enough, Cotillard plays it safe, Cillian Murphy was brilliantly cast, and Joseph Gordon-Levitt FINALLY delivers something good enough to take him serious as an adult and serious actor).

Also, some of the mechanics and rules of the whole dream world gets lost with the fast pace of the movie. Filming dreams is always a problem due to the nature of dreams, they are too abstract for movies - and unless you pull a Felinni and do one hell of a misce en scene, you are bound to fail, as people won't buy it. I couldn't quite buy the whole thing, but Nolan keeps the whole suspension of disbelief going on pretty well so the movie isn't ruined, or not even scratched.

But... while far from perfect, it was possibly along with Toy Story 3 the best movie this year, and one of Nolan's best effort, up there with Memento and The Dark Knight. Surely a movie you SHOULD NOT miss. It has its critics - just see the user reviews on IMDb - but that is the final stroke of genius on this film: you gotta be intelligent to appreciate it. Sheep-like-minded limited individuals will HATE it. And all I can do is smile as I see confused faces come out of the movie theater - poor, poor minds...

9.title: Be the subject of Inception
9.content: Inception is one of the movies that reveals itself by being unrevealed. Script for this movie was the best kept secret ever since first trailer went public, but now after seeing it for a couple of times, i really don't think that knowing anything about the movie could ruin it for you. Of course it is for the best if you don't know a thing about it... not even the idea for the movie... because it is a movie about ideas, right? It is. It is also more than that. Explaining the plot, telling it is a movie about dreams or it is an action or a heist movie seems superficial, after you see it, and especially after it affects you. IF it affects you. There are many people i know that really liked it, but weren't moved by it, emotionally or intellectually. But, majority will be. The movie works on so many levels, and with every twist and every new level of a dream you feel more for the movie and think harder about it. Yes the movie is very demanding, you might lose yourself for a couple of moments, but if you menage to find your own way out, you might get that feeling of catharsis. And I'm not using that word coincidentally. After seeing it for the second time that was the idea that i think stands in the very base of the motivation for the characters - catharsis. The fact that the film itself is packed with extremely well constructed action scenes and was done with a very high budget was, in my opinion, a very subtle way of hiding secret messages, emotions and human factors that are the true value of the movie. You are in for one hell of a ride with this movie, and that ride is not likely to end with the ending credits. It is a film that continues to live in your mind, thus justifying the line "Your mind is the scene of crime". The mysterious ending does not leave you with a sense of an unfinished project, but with multiple solutions. And every single one of it works. And every single one of it has its flaws. Just like decisions in life are never without doubt. Technically this movie was outstanding. Editing is perfect, it guides you through the toughest parts of the film to comprehend with ease. Acting is very appropriate, no overacting whatsoever, thus every single character gets to you individually and as a part of an interesting mind game that could be someones master plan. Talking about Nolan who was writer and director would be pleonasm. Every single praise that this movie gets is partially or more than often in its wholeness addressed to him. This movie is his construction, his maze, his link between the minds, his and yours. I give this movie 10/10 and do not want to compare it to other movies of similar genre or plot, because if you get into the movie deep enough, you'll see that there are no movies like this one. It is completely original and not a breath of fresh air, but a wind that you could have trouble sleeping with for couple of nights trying to figure out where is it blowing from.

9.title: Inception is Nolan's Best Write Yet...
9.content:
Christopher Nolan blazed on to the scene in 1998 with his film Following. Depending on who you are or how much of a Nolan enthusiast you are, you might have seen his first work, Doodlebug from the year before. Nolan's newest and probably most cleverly written film Inception, has Nolan exploring his own head and dimensions since his 1998 work. It's incredible how this writer/director has made such a name for himself in such a short period of time. Although all his works aren't magnificent (Insomnia being not one of his finest), he places a stamp and an edge on each of his works that makes the film completely recognizable as a Nolan film. Just look at his little film called The Dark Knight.

Inception doesn't rip off other films that are likely to be the comparisons like The Matrix, it reinvents a genre and almost recreates it as if we're seeing it for the first time. The synopsis was a big secret coming down to opening day and I did my very best to not know what the film was about. I'm proud to say I succeeded, and I will continue to respect any person who hasn't seen the picture yet and wants to remain in the dark. If people see the trailer or poster, you'll know it has something to do about dreams. That's a spot on description I might say.

The performances are not stand out, loud, or boisterous to be considered Oscar threats in the race for 2010 but they're accessible, respectable, and all deliver some great work. Star of the film Leonardo DiCaprio performs top notch and has landed himself into a great place as one of the best working actors in Hollywood. He's unstoppable as the tortured character "Cobb" and what his work does here is improve his chances at Oscar consideration, the question is what film will they embrace, this, or his earlier magnificent performance in Martin Scorsese's Shutter Island.

One of the best things about the film, besides Nolan's impeccable writing style, is his choice of constructing the best cast ensemble of the year so far. Supporting players are all on their A-game, showing charisma and emotional depth. The player most worthy and in the hunt for an Oscar nomination is Academy Award Winner Marion Cotillard who remains beautiful as ever but delivers her most terrifying portrayal yet. 500 Days of Summer star Joseph Gordon-Levitt has just made himself one of the coolest actors in Hollywood. His action scenes are the most dynamic and entertaining which makes him one of the more likable actors of the film. Ellen Page is fun, satisfying, and sufficient. Page has long left her Juno work behind her and is moving forward to be a more progressive and challenging actress. It's always so good to see Oscar nominee Ken Watanabe still working and showing great work. His breakthrough role in Edward Zwick's The Last Samurai was in serious danger of being his one-hit wonder, but he shows he's here for a while. Tom Hardy, star of last year's explosive British film, Bronson, has just established himself in the states of a capable and competent performer. Hardy is the topping on this sweet, sweet cake of a film. Cillian Murphy, like always, keeps his character at a distance from the viewers, only allowing us to see what he wants us to see. Murphy is the secret greatness in Inception. Dileep Rao (James Cameron's Avatar), Michael Caine (Oscar Winner for The Cider House Rules), Pete Postlethwaite (Oscar nominee, Jim Sheridan's In the Name of the Father), and Tom Berenger (Oscar nominee, Oliver Stone's Platoon) are all added surpluses.

Technical work here is breathtaking including Wally Pfister's incredible Cinematography, Lee Smith's perfect Editing, and Hans Zimmer's sensational score are the three most likely Oscar contenders and feasible frontrunners. Sound and Visual crew are right there and close behind to land themselves in serious contention.

But again, enough can't be said about Christopher Nolan. I see him finally holding an Oscar this year for his writing work here and I wouldn't count him out for a Directing bid either. He's in top form and with a Best Picture category expanded to ten, this is a film the fans and "regular" audiences can get behind to boost Oscar ratings.

Inception is sensational. The second best of the year (depending on who you are, Toy Story 3 may have this beat by a smidge) and Christopher Nolan's best screenplay of his career.

9.title: Breathtaking Cinema - Why we go to the movies
9.content:
Inception is wonderful movie that takes you deep into the emotional dilemma of a man who is coming to grips with his wife's suicide. The visual medium never "felt" so real as you're presented with scenarios that draw out Cobb's feelings as he travels on his journey towards acceptance.

While much has been said about the on-screen plot, the emotional plot is what drives this movie. We're presented with visuals where the on-screen action is merely a trigger for deeper emotions. Take Mal's suicide scene with facing duplicate hotel rooms (one trashed, one in perfect order). It's easy to sense the symmetry of love and how Cobb felt helpless to watch half of himself die (as Mal says to Ariadne a half of a whole). It's obvious this isn't how Mal died, but you can feel the sense of concern, anger, sadness, helplessness, pain and emptiness that Cobb feels just from living through that scene. This is cinema at its best.

The two key elements that codify the ideas of the movie are held in two riddles: 1. The "Travelling on a train" riddle, which signifies the idea that Cobb had embedded so deeply into his mind that he and Mal would grow old together (the idea that like a virus was embedded deep into Cobb's mind) and 2. The "leap of faith" riddle which ends appropriately with "or become an old man, filled with regret, waiting to die alone" (Cobb knows he has to move on but has to travel the journey of denial, anger, bargaining and acceptance (which is what each level of the dreams represented) to get there.

To fully deal with her death Cobb had to realize that Mal did spend her whole life with him, but he can no longer live on just that memory of her and has to move on for the kids and himself.

The whole movie was a dream until he awakens on the plane surrounded by strangers he incorporated into his dream during the flight (he never talks to them and they never act like they truly know him). As Mal said it best "Feeling persecuted ... being chased around the world by anonymous corporations (wouldn't any husband feel people must blame him if his wife committed suicide?) ... I'm what's real" ... and she truly was.

This movie will be amongst the classics for a very long time.

9.title: Nolan's greatest film, and one of the greatest films of all time

If you are familiar with Nolan's work (the good Batman films, The Prestige, memento etc) then you will know that he tends to not let up on the audience and even when people are simply talking, he can have a tendency to keep the pace up and some how the adrenaline of the audience, its as if there is a fight going on, with words. the score was done by Hans Zimmer, who had previously worked with Nolan on Batman Begins, and the Dark Knight, which by the way are the two films with my favourite soundtracks. The music helped to keep the pace up when things seemed to slow down and would engage the audience telling them that 'something is about to happen'

overall this film was fantastic, I cannot wait till I see it again, and I can't wait until the Blu ray comes out. I can leave it up to you to device whether you agree with me or not, but trust me to go and see it.

9.title: An excellent thought-provoking sci-fi thriller from Christopher Nolan
9.content:
With the onslaught of dumb action movies that came out over the last 2 years, Inception is a welcome to return to the Hitchcock style of intelligent suspense and drama.

Every actor in this movie gives an incredibly strong performance, i've never liked any film Leonardo DiCaprio has been in before (except for Gangs of New York) but this gave me new found respect for the man. But Joseph Gordon-Levitt steals the show, he's really witty and a great person to watch. It's a shame that DiCaprio's character took the spotlight so much, i would have loved to have seen more of Gordon- Levitt's character.

The story and plot is extremely complicated and may take 2 viewings to completely understand, many previews claim Inception is a "heist" film, it isn't, the heist is not even the main focus of the story. The Main plot it about the power of an idea, how it interweaves with memories and dreams, and how an idea can make/break someone's life.

The Special Effects are incredible, but the really big special effects scenes are obvious IMAX moments that Nolan has a habit of making (think back to The Dark Knight when Batman was in Hong Kong and the camera panned around him stood on a skyscraper). There are plenty of scenes that use Slow-Mo, but the plot justifies it so it doesn't seem like a tired action gimmick completely. My favourite scene from the whole film is when Arthur (Gordon-Levitt) is floating around a hotel in zero gravity, and fighting with some bodyguards along the way.

The film was not completely flawless, the film was saturated with technical jargon. The film sometimes slowed down to a standstill to explain how it works, it's this problem that leaves no events of this film to the imagination (except the ending). This overuse of explanation is what makes the film so long, but the movie needs this explanation to keep people interested and not make them lost in the plot. I also didn't like the scene on the snow base, it seems in movies there's only so much that can be done on a snowy mountain. The ski chase is right out of Thunderball, oh and guess what, there's an avalanche too, it just had a few too many clichés But the biggest problem is the very end of the film, i personally didn't mind it, but my friend almost screamed with frustration at it. leaving something open to interpretation is all well and good, but when the film closes on it with no explanation when everything preceding it was explained into oblivion, it sticks out like a sore thumb and leaves some people alienated. It's easy to see why people hated the ending, they wanted a legit answer for the 2 and a half hours they just watched.

All in all, it's a great movie, not perfect, but it's going to be remembered as one of Nolans best, one for the intellectuals who love movies and love pulling them apart to analyse them.

9.title: Nolan's Gift

There's was a lot to talk about on the drive home, and I see the IMDb board is buzzing with speculation on what happened, particularly the ending. You could probably watch Inception half a dozen times sussing out the fictional technology that was at its heart, the hidden meanings in some of the dialog, the multiple layers upon layers in which the plot took place.

My take was less concerned with the details. I went into this viewing expecting an inspired film experience created by a modern master. And I wasn't disappointed. I found the cinematography on par with (and no doubt inspired by) Hitchcock's classics like North by Northwest and Vertigo. It should win an Oscar in that category. The score was fantastic. However, when they are tasked with the near-impossible mission of "inception", the planting of an idea in a person's subconscious, the team finds themselves navigating a complex web of dreams within dreams. The film is a thrilling and thought-provoking ride, exploring themes of identity, memory, and the power of the subconscious. It's a movie that rewards repeated viewings, as new details and layers are revealed with each rewatch. Though the fast pace of the film renders the significance of certain details, such as the organization who hired the dream stealers, the totems and how Saito was targeted in the first place was dimmed -- possibly a deliberate motive to keep us guessing or unraveling its ambiguity. this film may be an exceptional thriller, but it is certainly not qualified to be an exceptional dream film, as compared to say, Mulholland drive or Donnie Darko. I have yet to see a perfect dream film anyway.

This is because Nolan placed too much logic in a realm where dreams are supposedly logic-free. For instance, projections do not necessarily die after getting shot in a dream right? The actual 'dream' could have started anywhere in any point in the film (there was a scene where Leonardo's totem spinning was interrupted and he never spun again aside from the limbo scene). Nolan successfully placed his audience in a state of limbo, literally.

9.title: A theory
9.content:
Inception...a movie that is defined a lot by its amazing soundtrack (especially "Time" by Hans Zimmer). On the surface, this movie is about the Inception in a young tycoon's heir's mind. But actually, you can forget all of that. None of it is real...

From the moment the film starts, what we see is merely a dream. The dream of Dom Cobb, a man tormented by guilt. The Inception? It's actually for him! He's trying to plant an idea in his own head. And he's dreaming the whole time.

His team? All just projections of his mind. Some with telling names (Ariadne, who found her way out of a maze by using red yarn), some with less telling ones (Saito meaning purity, wisteria).

The movie gives you many hints. Dom says he doesn't like trains early on. Saito tells him he must take "a leap of faith", just like his wife did. His father in law tells him "it's time to return to reality". The old man in Mombasa grins and replies (when Cobb said it's the only way to dream in the "dream" den) "You should know/you're one to talk". The Cobal agents who attack him in the city seem to behave and appear in a similar fashion as the one's in Fishers dream, seemingly appearing out of nowhere and not being influenced by what's going on around them.

Dom is a broken man. It isn't quite clear (to me) if his wife did indeed kill herself. If she did, maybe she did so more over him not being able to return to reality (so the opposite of what he accuses her of). Isn't it odd that when he comes in the hotel room, she is in a whole different building? That's a lot like it might be in a dream...as in that it makes no sense, but somehow does.

The whole totem thing...first of all, Cobb's totem isn't his, it's Mals. It doesn't matter in the least how it behaves, because only Mal would know what it meant. Spinning forever or toppling, either way is just another sign that Cobb is dreaming.

The number 528 491 also keeps appearing throughout the movie. "528" is the harmonic frequency for the note "mi". The harmonic scales were developed in monasteries - "mi" is for miracles.

491 is the unforgiveable sin. (The Lord would forgive you 7 times 70 times.)

So Cobb descends to Limbo due to his guilt, but rises out of it by the miracle he creates (which is the inception that he now thinks that he was dreaming and woke up, but sadly, that's actually a lie).

Finally, the score to me is the last huge hint. Hans Zimmer's "Time", played over the final minutes of the movie has such a heartbreaking intensity and vibe of sadness, it just doesn't fit with a "happy" end.

But that's the point the film is trying to make. Happiness is what we perceive as happy. Cobb is continuing to live a lie/dream. But it makes him happy. It still is sad though, because there might be a real Mal and real children waiting for him in the real world. But he just can't come back :(...

9.title: A movie all Sci-fi fans will love...
9.content:
The movie has lots of action and fantastic CGI. For its time, it truly is a marvel of CGI and not only that, but it explores a topic and uses a plot-device that has never been explored before ie. dream dimensions, memory manipulation, dream death, and a unique type of 'PTSD memory' that can haunt a person for the rest of their live.

The movie is essentially a 'heist movie' almost like the Italian Job or Oceans 11, but they're not stealing anything... it's just really refreshing to see a film do so many unique things isn't being done by anyone else.

Needless to say, Leonardo does a great job leading the movie, and along side industry veterans like Ken Watanabe, Joseph Gordon-Levitt, Marion Cotillard, Ellen Page, Tom Hardy, Cillian Murphy, Tom Berenger and Michael Caine, the performances are simply outstanding all round (though an 'action movie' like this doesn't leave much room for any dramatic acting).

Overall, this movie is comparable to The Matrix, for it's action-packed plot and fantastic CGI as well as dealing with a unique subject matter. It's WELL worth the watch.

9.title: Inception, on at technical level, is nearly flawless
9.content:
Inception, on at technical level, is nearly flawless. The editing is brilliant, and he's able to weave all these different story lines so seamlessly to make something so amazing. The cinematography is the best it's ever been for Nolan. The stylish aesthetics, the smart use of lighting (such as the way Nolan makes the distinction between certain scenes in dreams vs reality), the amazing production design, etc.

The script, as well, is absolutely brilliant. Reportedly, Nolan had been writing this screenplay for roughly 10 years, and it shows. Everything is paid off here. Every single concept that Nolan introduces from the totem to the kick to the music, and everything else introduced. It's brilliantly structured as well. A film like this could truly have been a confusing mess of a film in lesser hands, but Christopher Nolan's steady and in-control direction keeps us from getting left behind. We're constantly able to follow the story along. Cobb as a character is complex and well-rounded with relatable and interesting motivations that keep the audience engaged throughout the entire runtime.

The cast is all great. Leonardo DiCaprio gives, once again, another great performance as Cobb. He beautifully depicts the conflict within this character, the endless amount of guilt that he feels for his wife's death. He feels guilt and even though we don't know why, we can see it on his face. And the rest of the cast is great as well, with a personal favorite being Tom Hardy's Eames.

The movie has some interesting kinds of layers to it. It's a story about dreams and reality (quite masterfully depicted, as you are forced to pay attention to follow what is and isn't a dream), an allegory to movies as well. The film makes an argument that in face of uncertainty, one should take a leap of faith, something repeated throughout the film, and embodied through its ending as Cobb walks away from the top letting it spin to its heart's content. But for me, what made this movie so amazing was the story of a man moving beyond his obsessive guilt over his wife's death, and getting back to his children. The emotional core of the story is that, and it's what makes Inception such a while journey.

Inception is also the Nolan movie I've re-watched the most besides only one other, and for good reason. There's so much to unpack in this film from the themes, philosophies, and ideas used, to the jaw dropping spectacle shown, Inception is a highly re-watchable movie that never gets boring.

9.title: Inception provides the kick of the summer
9.content:
When the credits began to roll, the audience groaned and then applauded. It was the opening night of Inception, the latest film from director Christopher Nolan and also the most anticipated movie of summer 2010. Expectations had been sky-high, and despite the excellence of Toy Story 3 and positive reviews for a number of other films, many had dubbed Inception as the picture that would "save" the summer. As people headed out of the jam-packed theater, a buzz filled the air, an electricity of excitement that I had not sensed before. It was the sound of people who had just witnessed something special.

The film opened with possibly the most confusing first twenty minutes I've ever seen. However, before I knew it, I was sucked into a world of intrigue, suspense and wonder. Describing Inception to those who have not yet seen it is nearly impossible: you have to see it to believe it.

To communicate his vision to viewers, Nolan selected an all-star cast that had the heads of some cinema lovers spinning. As our main protagonist Dom Cobb, Leonardo DiCaprio portrays a man who uses poise and experience to disguise an underlying tumult of emotions and conflicting motivations. Using minute body gestures and subtle facial expressions, DiCaprio reveals Dom not as the leader we initially imagine him to be, but as someone tortured by memories and regret. Though DiCaprio gets the juiciest character arc with a role that could possibly earn him some awards buzz, he is backed by an ensemble of equally strong performers. Ellen Page proves that she can rise above and beyond a certain wise-cracking, pregnant teen, while indie favorite Joseph Gordon-Levitt breaks out with his first major role in a blockbuster, providing a voice of reason and occasional humor while committing regular acts of badassery. Continuing her effort to connect with mainstream America, Marion Cotillard succeeds brilliantly as Mal, Dom Cobb's mysterious wife, alternating between disturbing intesity and heartbreaking emotion; she makes a convincing sometimes-antagonist but we never doubt the relationship between her and DiCaprio. In addition, Ken Watanabe overcomes an occasionally muddled accent and, along with Cillian Murphy, makes the most of a significant though slightly less complex role. Finally, as Eames and Yusuf respectively, both Tom Hardy and Dileep Rao hold their own against their more well-known costars.

Of course, as anyone who has seen the trailers can vouch for, one of the main draws of Inception was the visual effects. Jaw-dropping shots of cities folding in on themselves and men running on walls and ceilings teased audiences, promising more trippy effects should those people attend the actual movie. They did not disappoint; there were times during my screening where people audibly gasped. Technicians worked CGI in with the live-action so seamlessly that, even now, I can't tell which was which. Sets of decaying cities, a chic hotel and others exploded with detail and realism, while the cinematography gave the film a sleek, modern aura that perfectly fit the heist/thriller/sci-fi nature of the movie. Though there is no distinct, hummable melody, Hans Zimmer's score is outstanding, on par with the one he co-composed with James Newton Howard for The Dark Knight. It creates an atmosphere of tension that builds and multiplies through the entire film; it's noticeable without ever distracting from the film itself. The fact that, apparently, Zimmer composed it without seeing a single frame of the movie makes it all the more impressive. He also employs the French song "Non, Je Ne Regrette Rien" to eerie effect. Not only is it sung by Edith Pilaf, whom Marion Cotillard portrayed to great acclaim in 2007, but it also emphasizes many of the themes within the film.

None of this would have been possible, however, without the architects, director Christopher and writer Jonathan Nolan. Together, they build a reality with the imaginative scope of the greatest fantasy and sci-fi epics without sacrificing the emotional core of the film. They never forget that, no matter how lofty and ambitious the plot and ideas, no matter how mind-blowing the visuals are, no movie can succeed if it loses sight of the characters, of the human element. At the same time, they explore a concept that have enticed film-makers for generations: the nature of dreams and reality. They manage to explain the ideas within the story without ever slowing down the film. Instead of openly approaching issues raised by the illegal but seemingly commonplace occupation of extraction or "dream-stealing", they leave those discussions to the viewers, keeping the attention on the characters and story; every scene is pivotal to one, or both, of those elements. In relation to their previous films, Inception takes the psychological twistiness of Memento and combines it with the more escapist entertainment that was the Batman films.

Perhaps what makes Inception so extraordinary is, beyond the excellent craftsmanship behind it, the confidence it has in its audience. The film-makers, artists and other collaborators, even those behind the marketing and promotional campaign, refuse to accept the cynical myth so often regarded as truth that, especially of late, permeates the movie industry: that your present-day, average movie-goers are unable to recognize and reward good, intelligent film-making, that they enjoy only the familiar and commercial. Coupled with the box-office bang of Avatar (which I found captivating for the story and characters, in addition to the immersive, 3-D effects), Inception proves that movies can succeed without having a built-in fan base or a story based on previous material, that summer entertainment can be intelligent. It shows that originality is not a lost art in Hollywood, and audiences still appreciate smart, skillfully executed storytelling. Nolan and co. never condescend because they know and respect this. With Inception, Christopher Nolan keeps up his arguably perfect record, and after only a decade, proves that he just may be one of the best - if not the best - directors working today. He reminds us of the true power of film-making.

9.title: Christopher Nolan returns to his roots
9.content:
I just got back from the theatre to see this dandy little film hit the big screen, and I am just more than a little blown away. I won't say it's his best film, rather I think he improves a little each time, as every director aspires to do. Nolan has a gift for crafting scenes that stand alone, both humorous and engaging.

Inception has all the elements of Nolan's previous films. There isn't really anything new, and personally I found the twists rather predictable. However, for anyone who is tired of the internal drama circulating The Dark Knight and talks of a third installment, Inception delivers a light, often humorous, complicated and above all original storyline that centers around a thief who just so happens to specialize in extracting crucial elements from people's dreams.

But like the premise for Nolan's The Prestige and Memento, that summary is just the outer layer of this complex labyrinth of what should be another masterpiece to the Christopher Nolan collection.

The interactions between the Dream Team are absolutely priceless. They reflect the complex inter-relations of Insomnia. The father/daughter like relations of two of the team members to the resentful buddy-sort of sibling rivalry between others. Leonardo DiCaprio is on-top of his game as Dom Cobb...as expected, honestly. Joseph Gordon Levitt as Arthur is once again allowed to be funny and quick, whether showing the team's newest recruit, Ariadne (Ellen Page) the dynamics of 'waking' from the dreamworld, or creating a clever diversion to avoid detection. Tom Hardy as Eames plays the film's snarky BAMF, as a lighter protagonist that seems to offset Cobb's broodiness quite effectively. And Cillian Murphy gives one of his best performances of his career, especially in Fischer's last scene with his father.

9.title: a thinking mans fantasy!
9.content: in summer filled with crappy films n mindless stories inception stands out as it is one of the few films(apart from matrix)that mixed style with substance.i just couldn't help but clap at the end of the movie the sad thing was my fellow audiences didn't share my enthusiasm but its not meant for your avg dumb audience who loathes in mindless films.but for thinking audience this is like a buffet with all you can think theme.never before a movie made me so engaged in the dynamics of the plot that i almost forgot where i was as my mind was in a a race against the characters of the movie to breakdown the schematics of this labyrinthine yet emotional nature of the story unraveling in front of me.the story is so complex to explain that one needs a paper and pen to illustrate the ongoings.the actors were pitch perfect no complains about that. the screenplay is breath taking considering all the explanations that nolan gave i was never bored but intrigued.the set pieces were just jaw dropping and the photography of wally pfister just transcends you to the surreal world.being a huge fan of hans zimmer i had lots of expectations and he didn't disappoint but i feel he had less to do because unlike dark knight this film needed less elevation from the score as the story and screenplay were enough of holding your attention.yes,it does have some loose ends in being very complex rasing far too many debates about the ending.but i guess thats what nolan wanted us to do.kudos to nolan for coming up with such original idea.this is one movie you shouldn't miss it requires multiple viewings to grasp the idea.at the end of it i have only one question who is responsible for the "INCEPTION" of this idean in nolan's huge brain.

They so find themselves hired by a client Ken Watanabe wants them to enter the Subconscious of a target( Cillian Murphy) and implant a thought in exchange for Dobb having his criminal record erased as payment. Inception was a groundbreaking film it went beyond the scale of what was expected in taking the concept of dream and giving them this very complex premise but also leaves an impact thinking on about what you a just view. On such a creative scale after the Dark Knight, I have to say this is Nolan's biggest achievement despite all the criticism that it's too confusing. When the action does happen in the film it's insane the creativity of these sets built around the concept of the mind is amazing with the huge emphasis on practicality and CG. The destruction of dreams, buildings folding in on top of another. The fact that you do not just fight, but another event in another dream is also affecting the layout of the scene. Going from a straight hallway to wrestling in the air to the ceiling as the room spins. There are so many some of the best cinematography. All of it is even more immersive with Han Zimmerman's Soundtrack. The film is a breathtaking and magnificent experience and leaves you thinking back even after the story ends.

9.title: Inception - A Wavy Davy Review
9.content:
I am sick and tired of hearing rumours about Marvel or Universal wanting to do yet another remake or reboot. Surely after the disgust that was 'The Day the Earth Stood Still' remake, Hollywood would have realised how poor these kind of films are, but alas, no. There are still faint rumours that the Hulk franchise might be rebooted AGAIN...

So Christopher Nolan has created something so fresh, new and exciting that I must praise him to the heavens. The idea is simple: what if you could enter someone elses dream and find their subconscious thoughts. The film, however, becomes much more complicated.

The best in the world at this process of 'extraction' is Cobb (Leonardo di Caprio), who goes into the minds of certain targets in order to obtain valuable secrets. He must alter his process to Inception, which involves planting an idea in someones head, rather than stealing one. He and his team (Ellen Page, Joseph Gordon-Lewitt, Tom Hardy, Ken Watanbe and Dileep Rao) must carry out this final job in order for Cobb to be allowed back into the United States to see his children.

The film is quite complicated, admirably, but it is not nearly as difficult to follow as many reviews have stated. If you are watching with a good amount of attention, it should be easy enough to follow, even if it takes a few minutes to understand some of the more confusing parts.

Di Caprio is not completely engaging in the emotive action (mainly revolving his deceased wife played by Marion Cotillard), but he does a very good job all the same, and makes a believable action star. Ellen Page is slightly miscast as the teams 'architect', as she does not carry off the thoroughly intelligent look. Joseph Gordon-Lewitt and Tom Hardy are most impressive as slick team-players, and it is a shame they are not developed more than Lewitt's slight romance with Page and Hardy's slight rivalry with Lewitt. Michael Caine pops in for a neat cameo, too.

The film manages to convey the grand-nature of how our dreams feel through a number of set-pieces. I find it baffling that some critics say that Nolan misses the fact that our dreams are not so clear, and instead are very hazy. This argument does not make sense to me since when we are in the dream, it feels completely real, and so Nolan's vision makes sense. I'd say this film is more engaging than the Dark Knight, as it does not feel so overlong and overbloated, and manages a very, very good ending which makes you feel good and then suddenly makes everything dubious...

Go see it, you'll love it!

9.title: The Story of a Man Confronting his Demons
9.content:
The FAQ section on IMDb on this movie is quite extensive and practically covers every aspect of this film. It is also interesting to note that it also outlines Nolan's ideas behind the film, in particular that many of the ideas come from a book called 'A Course in Miracles'. While Nolan says that the idea behind this film is original, there are aspects of this film, such as the nature of the dream, and the question of whether we are living in a dream world, that has been explored in earlier movies, such as 'The Matrix' and 'Total Recall' (the 1989 version). Then there is the question as to whether the entire movie exists within a dream, or whether the dream sequences are only those sequences in which we are told as dreams. This, however, is discussed in the FAQ, and I will leave it up to you to read that for yourself.

The main theme that I got out of the film, and after reading the FAQ, I have come to understand that this is the theme that Nolan intended, is the story of a man who is confronting his demons, though the FAQ more accurately describes it as guilt. The idea is that we are burdened down by the guilt of our actions in the past and until we are able to confront them, and forgive ourselves for them, then they will continue to burden us. We can respond in multiple ways, including blaming others for these events, beating ourselves up for these events, or simply accepting forgiveness (in whatever sense that forgiveness is offered). In the film it is clear that Cobb is beating himself up, despite him actually being innocent in the whole affair.

Using the concept of shared dreams, and the vehicle of science-fiction, Nolan explores how the guilt of our past actions continues to haunt us. In Cobb's world this is the continual emergence of Mab, and also of his children, and at one point, the train that goes flying through the middle of the city street. It is clear that Cobb holds himself responsible for Mal's death (which, interestingly enough, means 'evil' in the Romance languages – most likely representing the evil that we have done in our past, or the evil that has been done to us, which in turn burdens us down). As is also clear in the film, it is the act of forgiving, whether it be forgiving ourselves, or forgiving the perpetrator of that evil, that enables us to free ourselves from that burden.

Another idea is the idea of inception. This idea is that a little seed that is planted into our mind, usually subconsciously, can grow to change our entire character. In many cases, it is implanted into us in a dream, but in doing so, it can send us off into a dream state, and result in us being unable to differentiate truth from fantasy. It can work in two ways though, and in one way it can simply be a means of oppressing and enslaving people. For instance a bully can use inception to convince you that you are not being bullied, and that the bully is actually looking out for you, and by giving yourself over to that idea, you in turn become a slave to the bully.

This idea comes over to the dream world as well, because when we become the subject of an inception, we end up becoming trapped in a dream world. Now in saying this I am not necessarily attacking post-modernism, but rather an extreme form which suggests that the only reality is that reality that we create for ourselves. There is the idea that everybody experiences reality differently, but there is another, extreme view, that the only true reality is the reality that that one particular person experiences, and that if somebody does not submit themselves to that reality, then they are living in a dream. What post-modernism does is not justify everybody's individual realities, but accepts that the world, and the events in the world, will be view differently by different people. One person may enjoy a party, but another person may hate it, however, if the person who hated it insists that everybody who enjoyed the party is delusional, then that is the person who is trapped in a dream.

9.title: Perhaps I misjudged this movie.
9.content:
So, I made a mistake a few years ago. I watched this movie when I was barely able to even pay attention to it. I never understood it. Thinking on two or three levels at a time is just a lot for me I guess. 9.title: The film makes people think outside of the box.
9.content:
Inception is a movie about Dom Cobb (Leonardo DiCaprio), who is a thief of different kinds. A thief who commits espionage by entering the dreams of the people he is targeting. DiCaprio and the people he works with enter the dreams and use dreams within dreams to complete their tasks. Once they have obtained what it is they need they wake themselves up by falling or dying in the dream. The main person they are targeting in the film is a Japanese businessman, Mr. Saito (Ken Watanabe) who eventually has DiCaprio and a few of his accomplices (Joseph Gordon-Levitt as Arthur, Cobb's partner; Ellen Page, Ariadne, the architect; Tom Hardy, Eames, the fence; Dileep Rao, Yusuf, the chemist) attempt to plant an idea in the businessman's competitor's son to ruin his father's business, also known as inception.

Before all of this had occurred DiCaprio was facing a murder charge in the U.S. and was unable to return, Mr. Saito told him if he could pull the inception off, he would use his powers to clear Cobb's name. After going through many different levels of dreams to get deeper and deeper into the thoughts of their target and achieving inception, and after many different types of "kicks", which brings a person out of a dream, the members of the team get back to reality. Mr. Saito kept good on his promise and Cobb was able to return to the U.S. This makes the theme of this movie a focus on style or texture or structure. The film has a strong impact on the viewer's minds and senses.

The film makes people think outside of the box. No one really knows what causes dreams or the meaning behind dreams. This film makes us think about what could actually go on inside of a dream. Many of the ideas in this film make us think about every aspect in our dreams, such as the feeling of falling in a dream or having a dream inside of a dream. Another film that has this same kind of theme is The Matrix. The Matrix depicts a reality felt by humans that is actually a simulated reality. This movie also has a strong impact on the viewer's minds and senses.

The lighting in the movie, Inception really makes it feel like a dream. The lighting is often dreary and kind of dark, almost like an actual dream. The skies are often overcast and the sun doesn't shine much in the movie. These lighting aspects make it feel even more like a dream. The sounds in the movie also make it feel more like a dream. There are out of this world sounds throughout the film and sound effects that are out of this world that make it feel even more like a dream.

This movie made me think a lot more about dreams and wonder more about the real cause and meaning behind dreams. It also has made me put more thought into dreams within dreams. Every time I have a dream within a dream it reminds me of this movie and makes me wonder what the dream might have actually meant. Movies like this aren't just for entertainment purposes, they also make a person think about life.

Some critics have have tried to point out the frustrating aspects of the movie in the form of self explanatory rhetoric in order to describe what's happening, some what similar to "Memento(2000)"; I beg to differ. Cillian Murphy,Ken Watanabe,Joseph Gordon-Levitt,Tom Hardy are simply superb. I especially likes JGL and Tom Hardy's stints.

The Direction is great.....I am just getting tired of writing Good , great again and again.

Catch it at all costs.
