9.title: Extremely Interesting and Still Entertaining
9.content:
I'd been told this movie was very forgettable and not really anything special, but I owned it so I thought I should probably watch it. I was and wasn't surprised to find that it was very close to perfection.

Inception is not a movie where you can afford to zone out. You need to pay attention to get the full enjoyment out of this film. I found that I still zoned out at times, but nevertheless understood most of it and was able to enjoy it immensely. It's epic, with interesting characters and a very unique concept.

However, it takes more then a good idea to make a good story. Inception, however, had both. It set itself up to be an epic, yet complicated, movie, and thus it succeeded. It showed the audience that it would be part action right away, which allowed it to make more sense for the plot to involve a good amount of action, and largely revolved around that. Christopher Nolan knew what he was doing with his idea, and that's something that can be hard to find these days.

Overall, Inception is great. I've heard too many people I know say its dumb or nothing special, but I feel like they say that simply because it got high ratings that they may not entirely agree with (or to be the devil's advocate). But when you get down to it, Inception is fantastic. The visuals are great, the concept it great, and overall it's just really well done. Sure, the characters could use work, but that's about the only place where the movie lacked. If your looking to sit down for over 2 hours to think and enjoy something epic, then look no further then Inception.

9.title: I'm blind and I still understood this movie. Well done, Nolan.

Here's a rare treat. An action movie with a great script. Nice going "Inception".

There were parts of this movie, I'm telling you, I had not a clue as to what was going on. But, here's the thing, I think sighted people had the same problem. You just have to wait and it all gets explained for you. It's okay sighted people. I know, I know. Ssshhhh. Ssshhhh. I got you. Ha ha.

The thing I like about a movie like this is you not only have to invent yourself into a situation but you also have to invent the way out. And that's a very cool trick to be able to do.

The atmosphere they created in the movie was incredible. A nice slow burn with the character development of the story arc and everything. How about Leonard o DiCaprio, huh. The cool thing is he's got a very human element to him in this film. He's just not one of these steely cold agents who can walk around and handle a gun. He's very much a human in this film too. It's great.

The music in the movie is incredible. Hans Zimmer who is one of my favorites is just amazing. What an atmosphere the music creates in this film. It really helps with the tension.

So it's an action movie, right? You know how these things are. There are these long passages where there is plenty of stuff going on but with no picture - all you hear is gun fire, screaming, a car chase, a little bit of grunting, some other human noises. But it doesn't matter because the way this movie is written they tell you after the scene what all the action was and explain it to you one more time. Nice job, Christopher Nolan. Seriously. Come on! You can do movies for me anytime. Ha ha.

9.title: Inception - Movie Review
9.content:
Inception is a heist film by Christopher Nolan. The movie is based on the philosophical subject called "Dream Argument". The Dream Argument essentially hopes to point out that we cannot distinguish between dreams and reality on the basis of perception. Anything we see, feel or hear might as well be the part of a dream.

The movie takes the Dream Argument to a whole new level by introducing dreams inside dreams inside dreams and more..! It may be said that people inside a dream share a "Dream Space". In the movie, Leonardo DiCaprio's character discovers a way to enter someone's subconscious mind and access his dreams. He uses this to plant ideas into people's minds and also to extract information.

The movie has action and mystery written all over it. It is also food for the mind as it forces the viewers to put their thinking caps. If you are willing to do the needful, this movie should be a treat to watch. In the end it leaves a question which many today try to answer. The film is unique with respect to it's theme and ideology.

9.title: A masterpiece that made me realize something. Fellow writers, read on. No spoilers.
9.content:
It's 2017 and I finally managed to watch Inception, twice at that. Seven years after its release, I don't think it's necessary to go over the qualities of this movie again and bore you with expletives and superlatives regarding its excellence. The rating and the rest 2000+ reviews can tell you enough about that. Instead, I decided to present you with a fresh view on Inception's essence - my own one. Stay with me and I promise you that by the end of this review, you'll see yet another layer of Inception you haven't even thought about.

After seeing Inception for the second time, I realized that the primary concept of the movie - ideas, is in fact an elaborate tutorial on writing fictional characters.

Inception explores ideas and the way they affect us. In our everyday lives entering one's dreams and implanting an idea would be an impossible task. However, there is one place in real life (or not so real life) where inception of ideas is inevitable - books.

The author of a book isn't much different from the extractors in Inception. Because the author always works within his character's mind. He must know who his character is better than anyone else, in order to know who they will become by the end of the story.

In the course of the narrative, the author leads the character along a path that foreshadows and shows them hints about the future outcome. Nothing else - just hints. The character must arrive at the designated outcome by themselves. Thus, they go through the specifically constructed challenges and obstacles, which urge them to look at the world from a different angle and maybe realize a thing or two about themselves and the people around them. The author never explicitly says "See what I did here? It's supposed to lead to this and that." because that would break the willing suspension of disbelief of both character and reader - it would draw attention to the writer. However, he covertly (and cleverly) weaves the path before his character and shows them the things that would make them question themselves and eventually lead to a change in their mindset.

Yet, what drives the character forward after all? Their goal. But, let's face it - no character goal is truly that character's personal goal. Literary characters are just that - fiction. In reality, goals belong to the author who masks them so skillfully that the character believes them to be their own. After all, goals are the embodiment of a character's hopes and dreams and although their material form is usually absent at the beginning of the story, the strive to achieve them gives the character strength and perseverance. And what else in the world is intangible, yet strong enough to affect one's life? Ideas.

If you are just reading books for enjoyment and not obsessively inspecting each sentence like I do, at the end of the story you will see a character that has altered their way of thinking, but you won't realize the process through which it had happened. They would have either reached their goal, or realized that it hadn't been what they actually needed. Anyway, they would be a "new person" - they would look at the world with clear eyes. When you trace it back in the story, you might be able to tell how and why (provided that you are skilled enough in literary analysis).

But why is it so hard to determine the trigger of character development WHILE you are reading? Let's make it clear - it's not because you're not paying attention. A badly written story will scream "THIS IS SUPPOSED TO LEAD TO CHARACTER DEVELOPMENT!" ten pages before the actual trigger. Then what is the secret?

The thing is, just major story events strung together can't lead to character development that feels natural and the story will start screaming for attention like I showed above. Moreover, characters will be one-dimensional, will seem to lack firm motivations and goals, and their emotions will feel forced.

The secret lies in the small details skillfully placed at just the right moments in the narrative, which build upon one another to lead to the major events. Thereafter, the major events have greater impact and resonate into character development. Amateur writers won't notice these essential small details unless they have trained themselves to spot them through reading. They will think that the major events are the only triggers of character development. Then they will write their own stories without these key details and wonder why they won't trigger the same emotions like their favorite novels. Why they won't trigger any emotions at all. Well, now you know why.

Anyway, I feel my review turned into a creative writing lecture, but Inception perfectly illustrates the way an author develops their characters. At least that's the conclusion I reached for myself and the way I saw the movie. Because I'm a writer and I filter everything through my own crazy, maniacal, writing prism. My review may not appeal to the people who came for the action sequences or the ones who simply wanted to enjoy a masterfully crafted story. However, I hope my point will reach those of you who are just as literary crazy as I am.

I would prompt you to read this review after you've watched the movie, so you can see the connection between what I said and what happened in the story. Though since I'm placing this paragraph at the end of my review, it would be foolish to ask this of you, won't it? Yet again, I would prompt you to reread it after you've seen the movie. Or at least, to go into Inception with the idea in mind that it is an illustrative example of how to develop characters in fiction. The best of all examples.

9.title: The first great film of the decade
9.content:
With Inception, Christopher Nolan carries on his great work from both Memento and The Dark Knight, and the result is like a cerebral Bond film (indeed, the ski chase seemed like a rather overt homage); it has the complex narrative structure of the former by deviating from conventions in both time and space, and at the same time the unusual ambition and explosive action of the latter. Furthermore, I think he managed to pull it off in both aspects excellently.

With a whole dream (within a dream (within a dream)) world to explore, it would have been easy for Nolan to resort to sheer tricksterism. While it does feature some amazing effects, like the rotating hotel and a city folding in on itself, it does not really come across as showing off.

A common complaint about Inception seems to be that the first half spends too much time lecturing its audience on how dreams work and what can be done in them. While it is a rather extensive segment, I found it highly entertaining even on repeated viewings, and it does help the film to delve deeper into Leonardo DiCaprio's complex character. Admittedly, it could certainly have been told in a more economic fashion, but in a grand film like Inception, it only seems fair that most parts are fleshed out – the second half provides more than enough action to satisfy the viewer anyway.

Another recurring complaint has been that the dream worlds are not dreamlike enough. Except for some minor details, the dream worlds do look a great deal like the real world, but I for one have dreams that resemble Inception a whole lot more than, say, Last Year at Marienbad.

That being said, Inception is certainly not without flaws. For instance, it's easy to succeed with the mission if you keep coming up with new rules for the dream worlds as you go along, and I also felt that most of the characters (save DiCaprio's) were sort of underdeveloped, but that would make sense if it all takes place in DiCaprio's dream, which seemed like one out of several possible interpretations. The rather subpar plot about trying to break up some giant conglomerate as well as the fact that the protagonist is being followed by a strange, underdeveloped corporation fits into that interpretation too. And in any event, this didn't bother me at all since it is such an intense and thought-provoking ride all along. All in all, Inception is probably the first really great film of the decade.

9.title: Awesome
9.content: Inceptions is one of the biggest hits of 2010 that will leave you questioning your own reality. Directed by Christopher Nolan, the film stars Leonard DiCaprio as Cobb, as a thief (extractor) that specializes in industrial espionage, but in a very unique way... he steals the information from his targets own mind in their dreams. Cobb is hired by Saito, Ken Watanabe, to pull off inception, or planting an idea in someone's mind. In this case Saito wants the son of one his business rivals, Robert Fischer (Cillian Murphy), to break up his father's company upon his death. In order to complete this job, Cobb needs the help of his five member team. The first team member is Author, played by Joseph Gordon-Levitt. He is the researcher of the team, and finds out all the details of the target to make the information extraction easier. The next member of the team is Eames played by Tom Hardy. Eames is the team's forger, which means he can impersonate anyone while in the dream world. The third member of the team is architect Ariadne, who is played by Ellen Page. Her job is to design the mazes in the dream world in order to give them extra time to complete the inception. Dileep Ra, plays Yusuf, the chemist and final member of the team who designs and administers a sedative that helps keep the team and the target asleep, while not diminishing brain functions. The main theme of Inception is that of emotional effect. This is most clearly demonstrated by how Cobb is portrayed in the film. He and his wife Mal, portrayed by Marion Cotillard, had previously been stuck in limbo. In order to get out, Cobb implants the idea in his wife head that she is stuck in the dream world. This works to well, and once they get out she is unable to accept that she is in the real world. She believes it so much that she sets up a scene of her "murder" and waits for Cobb to arrive. Then she tells him that he has to kill himself with her so they can go back. If not, he will be blamed for her murder and spend the rest of his life in jail. Cobb refuses to do it even as she jumps to her death. Cobb is now forced to be on the run and separated from his kids. Visually, Inception is very similar to his previous films of the Prestige, and Memento. They all have the dark color pallets, and intense visual images. One of the strongest visuals in this film is the mirror scene in the dream world. This scene hints that there could be infinite levels to the dream world. I believe it reinforces the idea that even the "real world" is also a dream world that Cobb is stuck in. The other effect worthy of note is the use of slow motion. I believe that the use of slow motions adds to the audience experiencing the time change compared to the dream world. Overall, I believe that the Inception is a visually stunning film that is definitely worth the 2 hour and 28 minute run time.

9.title: A Mind-Bending Masterpiece of Narrative Complexity
9.content:
"Inception," directed by Christopher Nolan, is a cinematic tour de force that blends a complex narrative, stunning visuals, and thought-provoking themes into a unique and captivating experience. Released in 2010, this film solidified Nolan's reputation as a master storyteller capable of merging intellectual depth with blockbuster spectacle.

The film stars Leonardo DiCaprio as Dom Cobb, a skilled "extractor" who enters people's dreams to steal secrets. The plot centers around Cobb's most challenging mission yet: not to extract an idea, but to plant one, known as "inception." DiCaprio delivers a compelling performance, skillfully portraying Cobb's expertise, as well as his tormented psyche haunted by memories of his past.

The supporting cast, including Joseph Gordon-Levitt, Ellen Page, Tom Hardy, and Marion Cotillard, are exceptional. Each actor brings depth to their character, contributing significantly to the film's intricate plot and emotional core. The dynamics among the characters, especially as they navigate the various layers of dreams, are engaging and add to the film's immersive quality.

One of "Inception's" most remarkable achievements is its narrative structure. The story is a sophisticated weave of multiple plotlines that unfold in different dream layers, each with its own set of rules and logic. Nolan's direction and the screenplay handle these complexities with a clarity and precision that make the film's intricate plot both understandable and compelling.

Visually, "Inception" is a masterpiece. The film's dream sequences are brought to life with stunning visual effects, particularly in scenes featuring surreal landscapes and gravity-defying action. The iconic "folding city" scene and the zero-gravity hallway fight are standout moments that showcase the film's innovative use of special effects and imaginative cinematography.

Hans Zimmer's score is another critical component of the film's success. The music is powerful and evocative, enhancing the tense and mysterious atmosphere of the dream world. The use of the slowed-down version of Edith Piaf's "Non, Je Ne Regrette Rien" is both clever and impactful, deeply integrated into the story's themes and plot.

"Inception" is not just a visual spectacle; it is also a film that engages the mind. It explores themes of reality, perception, and the power of the human subconscious. The film encourages multiple viewings to fully appreciate its depth and complexity.

The film's conclusion, which has been the subject of much debate and analysis, is a stroke of genius. It leaves the audience questioning and pondering the nature of reality, a testament to the film's impact and thought-provoking nature.

In conclusion, "Inception" is a brilliant film that combines complex storytelling, stunning visuals, and intellectual depth. It earns a well-deserved 9 out of 10 for its originality, execution, and the lasting impression it leaves on its audience. Nolan has created not just a movie but an experience that challenges and captivates, cementing "Inception" as a landmark film in the science fiction genre.

9.title: A Mind-Bending Thrill Ride into the Realm of Dreams
9.content:
The story revolves around Dom Cobb, played by Leonardo DiCaprio, a skilled thief who specializes in the art of extraction-stealing valuable information from people's minds through their dreams. Cobb is presented with an opportunity to perform the ultimate act of inception, planting an idea in the subconscious of a target rather than extracting one. As he assembles a team of experts, each with their unique skills, the film delves into the complexities of dreams, reality, and the blurred lines between them.

Christopher Nolan's direction is nothing short of masterful. He skillfully weaves together multiple layers of consciousness, seamlessly transitioning between dreams within dreams. The film's pacing is tight, maintaining a relentless momentum that keeps the audience engaged and on the edge of their seats. Nolan's visual style is stunning, with breathtaking set pieces and meticulously choreographed action sequences that push the boundaries of what is possible on screen.

Leonardo DiCaprio delivers a commanding and emotionally charged performance as Dom Cobb, a haunted and complex character tormented by his past. His portrayal anchors the film and brings depth and vulnerability to the story. The ensemble cast, including Joseph Gordon-Levitt, Ellen Page, Tom Hardy, Marion Cotillard, and Ken Watanabe, all deliver exceptional performances, adding layers of intrigue and complexity to their respective characters.

Inception is a film that demands active engagement from its viewers. It explores profound themes such as the nature of reality, the power of dreams, and the consequences of unchecked ambition. The screenplay, also written by Christopher Nolan, is a labyrinth of ideas and concepts that challenge our perceptions and force us to question the very nature of our existence. It is a testament to Nolan's storytelling prowess that he manages to strike a delicate balance between intellectual stimulation and visceral entertainment.

The film's visual effects are groundbreaking and seamlessly integrated into the narrative. The manipulation of gravity, shifting cityscapes, and surreal dreamscapes create a sense of wonder and awe. The practical effects add a tactile quality to the film, enhancing its realism and making the dream sequences feel tangible and immersive.

Hans Zimmer's score is a standout element, perfectly complementing the film's tone and amplifying its emotional impact. The music elevates the tension and adds layers of depth to key scenes, further immersing the audience in the world of dreams and the high-stakes heist unfolding on screen.

In conclusion, Inception is a mind-bending and visually stunning cinematic experience that pushes the boundaries of storytelling. Christopher Nolan's masterful direction, coupled with exceptional performances, a complex and thought-provoking narrative, and breathtaking visuals, make this film a true masterpiece. It challenges viewers to question the nature of reality, invites contemplation about the power of dreams, and leaves a lasting impact long after the credits roll. Inception is a must-watch for those seeking an intelligent and thrilling cinematic journey into the depths of the subconscious.

9.title: Movie of your dreams
9.content: Here I'll be reviewing Inception, a movie I just re-watched for the 3rd time a short while ago. Inception was the 4th highest grossing film of 2010 and 14th highest rated movie ever (according to IMDb) and is well known for it's beautiful imagery and complex plot. Inception follows Cobb (played by Leonardo DiCaprio), a man haunted by the death of his wife, who makes a living off of entering people's subconscious. When a wealthy man wants him to head into a young CEO's mind and subliminally make him break up his company Cobb assembles a team to do so. Little does he realize the further he goes into the CEO's subconscious the deeper he goes into his own. I think the actors did a brilliant job, from the big names of Leonardo DiCaprio (Titanic, Catch me if you can) and Michael Caine (The Batman Trilogy) to the lesser known ones like Ellen Page (who plays Ariadne). What I really liked about this movie is it keeps you guessing. Just when you start to understand what's going on it changes things up. Its dream worlds are brilliantly imagined and it's plot is well thought-out with all of its intricacies. Some of the scenes were even done with practical effects. For the fight in the hallway with changing gravity, they actually built a hallway and spun it. My biggest gripe with the film is the dialogue which, while well written, is filled with exposition at the beginning of the film and slightly awkwardly cut occasionally. Though with this sort of film this is a necessary evil and did have action scenes to break it up. I think the main target audience would be people who enjoy mind-bending thrillers and action movies aged (as the MPAA rating suggests) 13+. I give this movie a 9.5/10 and recommend it for anyone to see as it's one of the best of it's genre.

9.title: Inception
9.content:
Inception, finally I got to this, found the right time to jump into this incredible experience, and incredible it was. As far as stories goes this is one of Nolan's strongest, smartest and most engaging entries. Supported by a brilliant cast and fantastic performances, this movie doesn't do much wrong.

Directing, where to start, it's a feat, and I can't think of any other director that can pull this off as well as Nolan did. To also keep it digestible for the viewer, and still leave enough questions to ask after the movie without being frustrated is quite the feat. I went into this thinking it was going to be a chaotic puzzle that I'd have to read the FAQ afterwards to get my answers. But I never had too. If you stay engaged and keep your full attention the the movie, the first little bit might be a bit hard to latch on but once you're with it there's some small exposition lines that will put you fully up to speed and there was no more confusion for me. It was surprisingly easy to follow. That said. I'm familiar with these sorts of movies, directors like Aronofsky for example loves to play with time, bend it and shape it to surround it's story.

Besides the story, the technical marvels are incredible too. Whilst CGI looks mostly great. The practical stuff, which Nolan prefers, is where this movie shines, and why Nolan's movies feel like a remnant of the past, where everything would be practical, and your mind would just be taken aback by what just what you see. This movie does, and has too.. lean more on CGI. Which at the end was okay.

Music. The impression I got that this movie would be this bombastic horn blast was completely wiped away. It was a trailer thing back then. So I went in a little biased. But the score is incredible. And it's never bombastic, but it comes and goes at the perfect times.

Acting. DiCaprio shows some of his best, but the supporting cast is just as good. Everyone provides exactly what the movie needs and no-one feels out of place. Characters just as much. Excellent writing, DiCaprio's character being the highlight, his dynamic and complexity are the finishing touch to this mind bending spectacle.

One downside. And for such a large movie. It's commendable. But I found the action, well.. the shooting, and it's... irrelevance to become increasingly dull throughout the duration of the movie. The bad guys with guns, that seem to shoot blanks 99% of the time, get way too much screentime. Meanwhile the plotarmor stays strong. I was okay during the start, but especially the van scenes and the artic scenes were just pushing it too far. I wish they found a different solution than a lot of this ''cheap'' action. It hampered the great flow the movie had for me.

This is a movie you want to keep going (minus the mindless action shooting) because the world and the characters in it are just too good to leave. If anything.. we're all like Ariadne, after that first hit..

Fantastic, hope to rewatch it on a bigger screen in the future.

FILM: 9/10.

As I settled into my rewatch of the 2010 film Inception, I knew I was in for a treat. Amongst Christopher Nolan's filmography, Inception has always held a special place in my heart, and this viewing only solidified its position as one of my favorite films by the director.

The movie's scope is simply breathtaking, with a multi-faceted story brought to life by exceptional writing. As the intricate plot unfolds, I find myself eagerly connecting the layers of the dream world in my mind. It's a testament to the film's excellent storytelling that a narrative with so many realities is surprisingly easy to follow.

The visuals are nothing short of awe-inspiring. Nolan's attention to detail and ability to craft stunning visual spectacles never fail to impress, making the dreamscapes all the more immersive.

The cast is undeniably outstanding. Every member of the team delivers a remarkable performance, but Tom Hardy's portrayal particularly stands out to me. His charisma and talent add an extra layer of enjoyment to the film. Cillian Murphy's performance is another highlight, showcasing his range and depth as an actor. Leonardo DiCaprio, as expected, exudes maturity and brings emotional depth to his character. 2010 was a particularly good year for him between this film and his work in Scorsese's Shutter Island. Joseph Gordon-Levitt's steady presence is a perfect complement, while Elliot Page becomes DiCaprio's grounding force, providing a captivating dynamic between the characters. The only slight disappointment is Marion Cotillard's portrayal of Mal, as it leaves me a little cold, but this minor quibble doesn't detract from the overall brilliance of the film.

Hans Zimmer's score is an integral part of the movie's magic, and I find myself captivated by its charm and energy. 'Mombasa' and 'Time' are standout tracks that beautifully capture the heart and essence of the story.

Christopher Nolan's mastery is evident in every frame of Inception. His control over various elements - from storytelling to visuals to performances - is awe-inspiring. It is this control that solidifies his place as one of my all-time favorite directors. Inception serves as a masterclass in his filmmaking techniques, leaving me in awe with every viewing.

Inception remains a cinematic triumph that continues to resonate deeply with me. Its brilliance lies not only in its stunning visuals but also in its captivating writing, phenomenal cast, and memorable score. It's a film that keeps drawing me back for more, and I can confidently say that Inception will always hold a cherished place in my heart and movie collection.

9.title: review of review
9.content:
With a background in reviewing many different genres of movies, particularly: dramas, action movies, and thrillers, reviewer dvc5159 has a lot of experience in analyzing the skillful development of these types of films. This review praises the balance of the visual effects, amazing cast, stunning cinematography, as well as the blend of popular and artistic filmmaking. It is truth-filled in the fact that it also points out that "visuals and intelligence rarely come together in movies at the same time, it's either all-visuals-no-smarts ("G. I. Joe", "Transformers") or the exact opposite ("Doubt", "Invictus"). In this film the excellently directed action sequences combined with immensely groundbreaking and jaw-dropping visual effects are combined smoothly with a heavy dose of intelligence and believability." Having seen the G. I. Joe movies as well as one of the transformers movies I can vouch for the fact that they aim for a visual appeal and less intellectual appeal which leaves the viewer feeling slightly in need of the missing element. The same goes for the opposite types of films. There is no balance, and we can tell, unlike in Inception where we have a thought-provoking plot as well as amazing, M. C. Escher-like visuals. An important side note to be aware of is that dvc5159 has an obvious bias for Christopher Nolan movies (which I can respect) so this review ends up presenting a passionate appeal to back these opinions. Besides emphasizing the amazing cast, dvc5159's writes in his review, "Nolan is a genius and I applaud him for treating his audiences as intelligent people." This gives us the impression that this reviewer prefers movies that respect the dignity/intelligence of the audience. Although the review does go on to say, "Missing this film and not getting the film's point is a crime." Which also indicates that respect is lost if you do not share the reviewer's same level of understanding after watching this movie.

Dvc5159 does not delve into the plot of Inception, but he avoids doing so for reasons stated in the review. It says, "honestly I can't explain the plot for fear of spoiling the movie for you readers. Even the slightest hint will ruin the experience." So dvc5159 instead tries to inspire the readers to go see the movie themselves by listing the cast, highlighting the combination of intelligence and stunning visuals, comparing it to previous Nolan films, and praising the cinematography. The motivation for this review really comes from the reviewer's love of Christopher Nolan films and background/experience in reviewing movies, and subsequent desire to share this story with others.

Overall, I think that this was a really valuable review even if it did not specifically break down each scene. Thank you for this post.

9.title: Shutter Island meets The Matrix
9.content:
The title says it all, if you've seen both movies you'll have a good feeling for what to expect.

I have a tendency to pick apart unrealistic details in movies, so I kind of liked the fact that the entire premise of the movie was unrealistic with today's technology. It forces you to accept the reality that with specialized equipment and training, a person could construct an entire dream world, and bring others into that world without their knowledge. 9.title: Undeniably Gripping, Mind-Bending Masterpiece
9.content:
Christopher Nolan's Inception is a mind-bending masterpiece that's as intricate as it is entertaining. The film drops you into a world where dreams can be navigated, manipulated, and even weaponized-a concept that sounds like it could go off the rails, but Nolan steers it with stunning precision. It's smart without being pretentious, emotional without being soppy, and action-packed without feeling shallow.

Let's start with the standout: the visuals. From cities folding onto themselves to the gravity defying fight scenes in spinning hallways, every frame is meticulously crafted to draw you into this surreal dreamscape. The special effects hold up remarkably well, even years after its release. Hans Zimmer's score is another huge win, those booming brass notes elevate the tension to almost unbearable levels, creating an auditory signature that's instantly recognizable.

Leonardo DiCaprio delivers a layered performance as Cobb, a man tormented by his past while trying to keep his team and his sanity intact. His emotional struggle gives the film heart, which balances the heavier, sometimes cold, intellectual aspects. The supporting cast of Joseph Gordon-Levitt, Tom Hardy, and Ellen Page, add depth and charm, with Hardy stealing scenes as the suave Eames.

That said, the film isn't without flaws. The rules of the dream world can get murky, and at times it feels like Nolan is explaining instead of showing. The dialogue leans a bit too heavily on exposition, especially in the first half. Additionally, some of the emotional beats, particularly with Cobb's wife Mal, feel slightly rushed given the sprawling nature of the plot.

Despite these quibbles, Inception is undeniably gripping. It's the kind of movie that sparks debates, demands rewatches, and lingers in your mind long after the credits roll. The spinning top ending? Perfection (in my opinion anyway), it leaves you questioning everything while feeling oddly satisfied.

Overall, Inception is an ambitious, thrilling, and thought-provoking film that redefines what blockbusters can be. It's not perfect, but its imperfections almost add to its charm. A strong 9/10.

9.title: Phenomenal amalgamation of Ideas, Narrative, Character and Spectacle.
9.content:
What I love about Nolan's films are their versatility - each of his films feature varying balances of ideas, narrative, character and spectacle. In my view, Inception is the perfect balance of all four aspects.

Nolan's films are reknowned for their portrayal of his intellectually-stimulating ideas; but I what I love are not just the ideas themselves, but in the manner they are presented. In the case of Inception, the ideas correlate directly to the narrative structure. What I mean to say is that the ideas of Inception refer to the nature of dreams and reality, and those themes are very fitting in a story of subconscious extraction and inception, and dreams-within-dreams.

What I found compelling was the idea of distinguishing between dreams and reality. As an audience, we feel a great sense of discomfort as we ourselves don't know whether our characters are in a dream, or in reality. This creates an intense claustrophobia; a psychological claustrophobia that is similar to the mental state of Cobb; allowing ourselves to empathise with Cobb because we also feel his pain.

And that brings me on to my next point - Character. What I adore about Inception is the contrast of an intimate character study framed against a large-scale heist within multiple dream-layers. In the beginning, we find Cobb in a troubled and turbulent state; held back by the death of his wife. His guilt, and inability to let go and to move on, shackles him. His problem is completely internal, and in order to fix it he needs to delve into his inner depths, to go past layer after layer, and to get to the root of his problem - to confront it. What he needs to do in order to help himself, is ironically his trained profession: to delve into dreams-within-dreams. However, the greater irony is that Cobb doesn't use his his professional skill to aid himself, but rather to hide away from his problem - delving into the depths of another dream in order to escape his turbulent reality; to go to a world of disconnect.

I wrote earlier how Nolan effectively utilises narrative to help convey his ideas, but as you have read above, he also utilises narrative to aid in the writing of his characters.

Furthermore, if Cobb wants to get back to his kids, he has to fix an external problem; his wife has framed him for a murder he didn't commit. However, in order for Cobb to overcome the external, he must first conquer the internal: his inability to let go and to move on after the guilty death of his wife. As he embarks on the mission of Inception, it proves to be therapeutic for him: he confronts Mal in Limbo, he embraces and confronts the fact that the Mal he's been trying to re-live is his projection of her, not the real Mal. He overcomes his desire to live in these dreams of disconnect with her, and to fully embrace reality. He moves on from his guilt as he tells her straight in the eyes "I have to let you go".

As a result of his triumph over his internal struggle, Cobb succeeds in his mission of Inception, as he returns home to see his kids again. Personally, I like to believe that the ending is reality, rather than a dream because it is the ending that Cobb deserves - the positive catharsis, as the film puts it. It's an ending he deserves due to his conquering over his internal struggle; his struggle to confront his painful reality rather than hiding away in a superficial dream. But what I like most of all is that Cobb himself doesn't check to see if the spinner is maintaining its motion or if its about to fall - he doesn't care to distinguish between the harsh reality or the idyllic dreams, this is something he worked for and invested in - this is his reality, whether its a dream or reality.

Earlier, I mentioned the sharp yet effective contrast of an intimate character study framed against the large-scale heist set within multiple dream-layers. The last half of the film is absolutely breathtaking - that whole sequence is one of the most nail-biting and heart-racing moments I have ever experienced in a film. Lee Smith's inter-cutting and meticulous layering of scenes had me completely enraptured. The film's spell-binding nature is also fueled by the propulsive score of Hans Zimmer, and aided by the gorgeous photography of Wally Pfister.

Many directors have often made one of their films dedicated to cinema - their love letter to film. For Scorsese it was Hugo, for Tarantino: Once Upon a Time... In Hollywood, and for Federico Fellini: 8 1/2. For Christopher Nolan, it is Inception.

In one scene Cobb remarks that one doesn't remember the beginning of a dream, then goes on to ask Ariadne how they got to the Café. She is stunned, realising that they are actually in a dream. The same can be said for scenes in films. In every film, we are just dropped into scenes without knowing how the characters got to the location in the first place. We fill in the gaps subconsciously, in the same way how humans create and perceive simultaneously while in dreams. The dreams are films, an alternative state of reality; an alternate state of distorted time and imperfect perceptions of reality. It's a thought-provoking idea that has an impact in the way in which one views cinema and the immersive nature of it.

Inception is a film of perfect balance between ideas, narrative, character and spectacle. Each aspect is incredible individually, but they also compliment each other, resulting in an absolutely impeccable amalgamation of a film.

9.title: best movie
9.content:
"Inception" is a cinematic masterpiece that takes audiences on a mind-bending journey through the realms of dreams and reality. Directed by the visionary Christopher Nolan and featuring a stellar ensemble cast led by Leonardo DiCaprio, this film is a true triumph of storytelling and visual artistry.

Clocking in at just over 2 and a half hours, "Inception" is a labyrinth of intricately woven narratives that demand your undivided attention from start to finish. The story revolves around Dom Cobb (DiCaprio), a skilled extractor who infiltrates people's dreams to steal their deepest secrets. However, he's haunted by his own past and a tragic memory involving his wife, Mal (Marion Cotillard), which adds a layer of emotional complexity to the narrative.

The film introduces the concept of dream layers within dream layers, each with its own set of rules and physics. This multi-layered approach to storytelling keeps you on the edge of your seat as you navigate through the shifting landscapes of the subconscious. Nolan's script is a marvel of intricacy, blending psychological drama with high-octane action and intellectual depth.

The visual effects in "Inception" are nothing short of breathtaking. The zero-gravity scenes, the folding cityscapes, and the surreal landscapes within dreams are executed with such precision that they immerse you completely in this world of infinite possibilities. Hans Zimmer's score, with its hauntingly powerful horns, intensifies the film's suspense and emotional resonance.

What sets "Inception" apart from other blockbusters is its philosophical underpinnings. The film delves into the nature of reality, the power of the human mind, and the significance of dreams. It invites viewers to question their own perceptions of reality, blurring the lines between dreams and waking life.

The performances in "Inception" are top-notch. DiCaprio delivers one of his career-best performances as the tormented Cobb, while the supporting cast, including Joseph Gordon-Levitt, Ellen Page, Tom Hardy, and Michael Caine, provide outstanding support. The chemistry between the actors is palpable, adding depth to their characters and relationships.

"Inception" is a cinematic triumph that challenges the conventions of storytelling and captivates with its mind-bending narrative, stunning visuals, and thought-provoking themes. It's a film that lingers in your thoughts long after the credits roll, prompting discussions and debate. Whether you're a fan of action-packed thrillers or cerebral dramas, "Inception" is an absolute must-see that will leave you awe-inspired and craving for more.

With its combination of innovative storytelling, exceptional performances, and groundbreaking visuals, "Inception" is a cinematic experience that deserves every accolade it has received. It's a timeless classic that will continue to be celebrated for generations to come. Don't miss the opportunity to embark on this unforgettable journey into the depths of the human mind.

9.title: In a Nutshell: "Inception" (9.5/10)
9.content:
Inception...You think you know about dreams, think again!

8 years is how long it took "Inception" to cook in the head of mastermind writer, producer and director Christopher Nolan. During that time he has successfully served us with things like "Memento", "The Prestige", "Batman Begins" and "The Dark Knight". This picture is one of a kind to say the least and will undoubtedly be noted through decades to come.

Dom Cobb (Leo DiCaprio), a master dream invader, leads a team of thought manipulators each of his own specialty, through the ultimate mission of their craft. After many jobs of stealing corporate secrets, they're now assigned to be creators rather than thieves. They're off to implant ideas rather than taking them away.

A good story could always be a solid foundation to making a good movie, now imagine a story so genuine like almost nothing that's been told before. "Inception" is one of those films that are likely to go wrong, with an idea that could potentially have numerous loopholes unless written by someone like Christopher Nolan. The mind bending thoughts that you get throughout the movie keep you alert, attentive and almost on edge that you may miss something. But then again it's taken him all those years to produce that coherent script, how many times you think he has read and reread every scene?

Needless to say that this movie is likely to be on top of the nominee list for Film Editing at the next Oscars, other areas of film making have been presented in a, more than a world class, layout. Look at it this way, if it hasn't all come together, "Inception" would've gone straight to DVD. You hear a train cutting through a hot pursuit on a side street, and you think of sound mixing and editing. You see buildings twisted and world physics messed up, you think of visual effects. Let alone, the cinematography and the art direction that constantly stand out from the opening scene right through the last minute.

In many ways Inceptions's main feature is simplicity of complexity. More of that is obvious in the movie score. Edith Piaf's "Non, Je ne regrette rien" is featured as not only a song but a main factor in intensifying the story at some point. Take that tune, put it on a very low pitch and you've got yourself Zach Hemsey's Mind Heist which is the main Inception theme. That well distorted trumpet you hear in the trailer and all over the movie is none other than a tempo adaptation of Piaf's music. If time is slower during a dream, so should music. Talk about story coherence. Furthermore, Nolan simplifies the complex even in front of the camera many times, to name one, rather than using visual effect in low gravity scenes, he decides to put the whole set on hydraulics and spin it so that it'll look more real. Wait till you see Joseph Gordon-Levitt walk on the ceiling.

Having all, behind the scene, aspects as tight as they've been, Nolan's following mission was to put a team together in front of the camera. With roles high in diversity, choosing actors had to be anything but an easy task. It is established that Leonardo DiCaprio was Nolan's first and last choice for the role of Cobb, but he's gone through a whole list of names before choosing the rest. The way I see it, he made all the right choices. Joseph Gordon-Levitt was James Franco's contingency to play "Arthur". Ellen Page, our beloved Juno, who played "Ariadne", was considered among names like Emma Roberts, Rachel McAdams and more. And Tom Hardy "Eames", Cillian Murphy "Fischer" together with Oscar nominee Ken Watanabe "Saito" has successfully filled in their characters' shoes in a way that is up to the standards of something as big as "Inception".

More to the list of stars, Academy Award winners Michael Caine and Marion Cotillard each represent an important relationship to Cobb in "Inception". The later plays a very complex role from an acting perspective leading the audience through a roller-coaster of confusion and emotional disturbance; she nonetheless represents a very important side of the story that if talked about more, may spoil much, despite what master critic Rogert Ebert said about the movie being "Immune to spoilers".

From beginning to end, you don't get to turn your head. You're right in the creative hands of a film making genius who knows what your mind loves and feeds it. Exceptional talent surrounds every bit of this journey. Enjoying it is not an option, it's forced upon you.

In a nutshell, Watch it!

9.title: Very Good, but too long
9.content:
Cobb (DiCaprio) is an Extractor, who steals industrial secrets by getting into a person's dreams and getting what he needs. But, Mr. Saito (Watanabe) hires Cobb and wants him to implant (called inception) a notion in Fischer's (Murphy) dream to have him break up his late father's company or the whole world will be held hostage to the monopoly.

Watching Inception is like looking at a Picasso painting. You are not sure what you are seeing. You see some things you like, some you don't, and much (if not all) you don't understand. But, you keep looking to see if it makes sense to you. I'll leave it there.

There is a lot of gobbley-gook explanations psychiatrists would salivate at. There are dreams, dreams within dreams, and dreams within deeper levels of dreams within dreams. See? Once you get by the gobbley-gook explanations you sit and watch the movie like you watched an old Mission Impossible TV show back in the day. You are mesmerized. You watch wires being strung, explosive charges placed, monitors placed, needles injected, lies and other rationalizations being told. See, just like an old Mission Impossible TV show, except there are also tons of gunfire and car chases which MI didn't have much of.

But, the CGI and other special effects are simply fantastic and yes, these things are perhaps things you might see in dreams because – as you well know- many things are possible in dreams where the illogical become logical. Hey, this is a dream. Anything is possible. Things that don't make sense in the real world become real within a dream and they make sense. Perfectly logical. See?

The actors become intense and so do you and you are fully engaged now once the dreams within dreams start. All is good except for one thing: the movie is too long and you are looking for the end game. If they had cut 40-minutes out, this would have been more enjoyable. But, too much shooting etc takes its toll, and, this hurts any Best Picture Oscar nomination in my view.

There is no denying that Leonardo DiCaprio raises the performances of everyone around him and this is blatantly obvious and that's a good thing. One day Hollywood will see that he and Matt Damon (not in this movie) are Oscar worthy actors. One day.

After seeing this, I know 3-things: (1) If you saw this in a movie theater, you may be encouraged to take out the DVD and watch it again fast-forwarding thru the too many shootings, car chases and explosions. And, (2) When you next see a Picasso painting you may be reminded of this movie.

And, (3) You are going to try to control what you do in your dreams. Good luck with that.

Violence: Yes. Sex: No. Nudity: No. Language: Yes, just JCs and GDIs. No F-bombs.

9.content: We all know our imagination when used can come up some of the most amazing and wonderful things, things that can bring a smile to our face or even make us cringe in fear, the good thing about using our imagination though is it is us who is using it and in that way it is us who controls exactly what happens, the same thing in our dreams as well. We are the ones who control our dreams if we know how. Leonardo DiCaprio (Basketball Diaries, Titanic) plays Dom Cobb a man who with his partner Arthur played by Joseph Gordon Levitt (Mysterious Skin, Stop-Loss) are "extractors", people who can enter the dreams and sub conscious of the unwilling through some military experiment and gather information with their contract none the wiser. The duo is hired by Japanese business man Saito played by Ken Watanabe ( Memoirs of a Geisha, Batman Begins) to enter the sub conscious of Robert Fischer Jr played by Cillian Murphy (Batman Begins, Breakfast on Pluto) and get him to dissolve his dead father's company. If Cobb and his team are successful Saito will ensure the murder charge that Cobb is currently being hunted for (murdering his wife) is dropped and he can go back and be with his two kids once again. Cobb assembles a team ready to enter the 3 levels of Roberts's subconscious whilst he travels from Sydney to Los Angeles with the corpse of his father Inception is a film that if you look away for a second you are utterly lost, miss that one important sentence and you'll be left scratching your head wondering what the hell is actually going on. Is it a film that can hold your attention for the entirety or do you lose interest here and there and wonder what to buy in the supermarket once you leave the cinema? For me it was amazing, so far-fetched and over convoluted, so much bullshit and crazy ideas, so much imagination and wonder all in one very messy and crisscrossed package. I have seen this movie about 3 times now and it still confuses me, in saying that though I do still love it as well. Every time I have watched it I have gotten more and more out of it. I believe it to be the type of film where if two people sitting in the same cinema met after the film to have a coffee and debrief neither of them would agree on the same thing to which they had just seen anyway, both of them would have seen exactly the same thing but come to two very different conclusions. I believe personally that's exactly what Nolan wants from his audience with this film, he wants us (the audience) to walk away and tell each other our own ideas and theories and walk away totally bewildered. For that it works and it works so very well. The scenes set up in some of this movie are beyond imagination, there is one very amazing scene with Joseph Gordon Levitt's character that gives me tingles just thinking about it. Nolan is a very very smart man and no doubt has very big things to bring to the cinematic world. The ending by far is one of the most significant in the film I have my own ideas as I'm sure you will as well. I don't believe this is a film you would enjoy with anyone under 18 and then again even those over 18 without imagination and the ability to escape into a reality of complete amazement won't enjoy it either. Inception gets 4.5 BanShee Screams out of 5 only because there is still so much to it I want to understand and can't without getting Christopher Nolan to sit down and break it down for me even though I'm aware of how much that will kill the entire film for me.

9.title: Intelligent and gripping entertainment that remains with you
9.content:
What many have written as criticism for Nolan's latest cinematic endeavors, I applaud: Christopher Nolan takes himself seriously.

For me, personally, films that attempt to draw me into a story without requiring me to think or even to draw upon more profound emotions and/or intelligence don't remain with me for very long. I want to enjoy a movie in the theater or at home and then keep enjoying it because it's content or portrayal is so compelling that I find mind migrating back to scenes or experiences in the film.

I do enjoy sitting down to a fun, exciting movie solely for the purpose of entertainment. Inception, however, is not one of those movies.

Everyone has dreams. After watching Inception, I found myself musing on the impossibilities and possibilities of dreams. I found myself wanting write down my dreams more often. That's the kind of movie Inception is: the kind that becomes a part, even if it's a small part, of my life. It becomes a place my mind can roam to for engaging thought and feeling. If Christopher Nolan did not take himself or his films so seriously, I'm not sure this level of personal influence could be achievable.

9.title: Nolan knows this job.

Inception is a science fiction thriller film written, directed and produced by Christopher Nolan. In the movie, Dom Cobb, played by Leonardo DiCaprio, is a thief who offers a legal solution to a job that can penetrate the deep subconscious of the mind. Cobb's job is to enter another person's mind and plant an idea there (to monopolize).

Inception has an incredible script and directorial skills. The film surprises the audience with its complex storytelling. Playing with the concept of time, the film shows how difficult it is to distinguish between reality and dreams.

The visual effects in the movie are quite impressive and successful. The creative designs and action scenes of dream worlds fascinate the audience. Additionally, the music strengthens the atmosphere in the film.

The cast is also very successful. Leonardo DiCaprio gives an impressive performance as Dom Cobb. Other actors bring their characters to life with their acting.

Inception also stands out as a film that deepens through subtexts. It focuses on the thoughts between dream worlds, the perception of reality and the human subconscious. This makes the movie more meaningful and thought-provoking.

However, for some viewers the movie may be confusing and they may miss some details. Also, its 148-minute length might be boring for some.

Overall, Inception can be considered a fascinating movie with its creative script, visual effects, acting and deep meanings. Directed by Christopher Nolan, this film is one of the best examples of the science fiction genre.

9.title: Sophisticated Spectacle
9.content:
As many reviewers have noted, this summer movie season...well, it's almost not deserving of being called a summer movie season at all. Sequels. Remakes. Reboots. Rehashes. Re-what-have-yous. Granted, they were not all bad, but neither were they all good. Along comes Christopher Nolan, Savior of the movie universe, with Inception.

The psychological action-thriller centers on Dom Cobb (DiCaprio), a skilled "extractor". Cobb is a master of a specific kind of corporate espionage: he enters peoples' minds while they are asleep to retrieve secrets from their dreams.

Cobb and his partner Arthur (Gordon-Levitt) are approached by the wealthy Saito (Ken Watanabe) to perform "inception": planting an idea instead of stealing one. Their target is Robert Fischer Jr (Cillian Murphy), the son of a terminally-ill tycoon. Saito wants Fischer to disband his father's empire.

However, Dom is a deeply troubled individual, and with valid reason: he is wanted for the supposed murder of his wife Mallorie (Cotillard), and visions of his wife manifest themselves in the dreams Dom enters. Being a fugitive, Dom is unable to return to their children.

Dom assembles a team to help perform the inception, consisting of Arthur, college graduate and "dream architect" Ariadne (Ellen Page), "forger" Eames (Tom Hardy) who impersonates others within a dream, Yusuf (Dileep Rao) the "chemist" who formulates the drugs needed to enter the dream state and Saito himself, as a "tourist" in the dream world.

And then things get (even more) complex.

In many ways, Inception, despite its mind-bending premise, is classic Christopher Nolan. Memento, Insomnia and the Prestige all display similar traits in that they enjoy playing with the audiences' minds. However, Nolan is a director who learns, and after gaining the experience of the big-budget Batman films, is able to translate his ideas into mind-blowing spectacle.

Inception exemplifies the thinking man's blockbuster, and it is very rare that filmmakers of tent-pole summer fare treat their audiences like geniuses. After scores of films that are so painfully dumbed-down, it doesn't hurt to watch a brain cell-jolting flick like this one once in a while.

Inception operates on its visuals: the notion that anything is possible within the world of the dream allowed production designer Guy Hendrix Dyas to go wild. The film includes such scenes as an entire city folding in on itself, a freight train running through a city, an assault on a fortress that wouldn't be out of place in a Bond movie and a desolate, abandoned dream city filled with crumbling buildings. One of the many great sequences in the film is a zero-gravity fight scene performed by Gordon-Levitt along the corridors of a hotel. Even for audiences jaded by the proliferation of "wire-fu" since the Matrix films, it's exciting.

Inception's greatest asset however is arguably its emotional core that functions like a rope guiding the viewer through the labyrinth of story. Leonardo DiCaprio has carved a career out of playing emotionally-complex characters, Cobb indeed brings to mind DiCaprio's recent performance in Shutter Island. Cotillard is also commendable in that it's never easy to play a character who exists only as a figment of another character's imagination, and Cotillard does this hauntingly well.

The rest of the cast, too, is an iron-clad ensemble. There is literally not one weak link, everybody is perfectly cast. Gordon-Levitt especially seems to be emerging as a bona fide movie star, after making a name for himself in smaller character films. Watanabe manages to be dignified yet possess a misleading sinister streak as the employer and money man.

Tom Hardy is a hoot as the comic relief who is actually really useful. My favorite however (it could be just that I'm a 17-year-old male) is the lovely Ellen Page, who has no problems portraying the youngest yet deepest character in the film. My only complaint with regards to the cast is that Michael Caine, as Cobb's mentor and father-in-law, is woefully underused.

If you're tired of being insulted by blockbusters that throw money at the screen and hope it sticks, then treat yourself to one of the best cinematic uses of money ever. There's no shortage of spectacle or intelligence in what I can safely say the best movie of the year. And it's only July! Or is it...

9.title: A Mind-Bending Journey with a Few Complexities
9.content:
Inception (2010) is a visionary and intellectually stimulating film that challenges the boundaries of traditional storytelling. Directed by Christopher Nolan, this sci-fi thriller takes audiences on a multi-layered journey through dreams within dreams, pushing the limits of imagination and reality. Leonardo DiCaprio leads a stellar cast, delivering a compelling performance that anchors the film's intricate plot.

Visually stunning and conceptually ambitious, Inception is a film that rewards attentive viewing and invites multiple interpretations. The combination of Hans Zimmer's mesmerizing score and Nolan's precise direction creates an atmosphere of tension and wonder.

However, the complexity of the narrative, while impressive, can be overwhelming at times. The film's intricate layers and fast-paced plot might leave some viewers struggling to keep up, which is why I held back from giving it a perfect score. Despite this, Inception remains a remarkable cinematic experience that stays with you long after the credits roll.

9.title: Levels of dreaming, levels of reality
9.content: This is an extraordinary film based upon little-known information about consciousness and the afterlife. The film was written and directed by the remarkable British director Christopher Nolan, whose previous films have included such inspired, original, and challenging ones as FOLLOWING (1998, see my review), which was a work of pure genius, MEMENTO (2000), and THE PRESTIGE (2006). Nothing seems to be known about where Nolan obtained his information, but INCEPTION could not have been written without some pretty unusual sources, and one wonders whether he regularly consults psychics, or just how he went about his research. No other writing credit is listed for the film, so Nolan seems to have done all this on his own. The film features many fine performances, but there was one false note: I did think that the late Pete Postlethwaite was absolutely wrong for the role of the dying man, but then he really was dying at the time, and one hesitates to speak ill of the dead, especially of a man who bravely went on acting until the last moment of his life and who in that sense achieved a personal heroic stature in his profession, and is respected by all. Marion Cotillard was an inspired choice for the role of the dead wife, and her performance is suitably spooky, moody, and disturbingly atmospheric. She has us on edge all the time, which is appropriate to the story. Michael Caine has a cameo role, for which he was highly suitable. The Japanese actor Ken Watanabe has a prominent role in the film, and he does very well except for one thing, namely his mangled English. He really does need more speech lessons. It was not always possible to understand what he was saying. The film ultimately succeeds because of a very strong and commanding performance by Leonardo Dicaprio, who has matured into a very solid and believable leading man and is no longer the boy of yesteryear. He has obviously kept himself from going over the edge with youthful 'star vanity', and has concentrated on remaining a good actor for the rest of his career. That must have taken a very great deal of self-control. Ellen Page, best known for her title role in JUNO (2007), was a rather unobvious choice for the girl, as she offers no glamour and is very much a working actress who is far from being seductive and just gets on with her job. No director would choose her as the love interest in a movie, as she makes no hearts throb. But it works out well, as Dicaprio has to remain obsessively in love with the weirdly wonderful Marion Cotillard, and cannot be distracted by something cute in a skirt, or it would have ruined the story. Anyway, Page wears trousers all the time, just to be on the safe side and keep the temperature down. This film makes effective use of spectacular special effects, which must have required an immense amount of planning, and they are fantastically effective. So this film is a real phenomenon; score one more for Nolan. Some of the inspiration for the story comes from obvious sources, such as the highly-publicised work of American 'spooks' in remote viewing and attempts at directed dreaming. The extraction of information from dreaming people is a kind of natural consequence of such activities. But Nolan has gone far deeper, and this is very far from being a superficial exploitation picture based on familiar, if imperfectly understood, information from popular books. After all, what has been publicly revealed is misleading in two senses: first, we are encouraged to believe that all that 'stuff' ended long ago in the 1980s and was abandoned because it could not be controlled properly and was too frivolous, and secondly that it had no deeper relevance to the true issues of consciousness, the 'afterlife', and other levels or dimensionalities of existence which may intersect with or impinge upon what we naively imagine to be the sole 'reality'. It is wrong to assume that 'other levels of existence' would be wholly immaterial, as there is a great deal of evidence to make it clear that 'the spiritual' is not 'immaterial', and that there is no pure Cartesian dichotomy between what we falsely call 'matter' and 'spirit'. The Chinese had a better understanding of the issue, as they never adopted such a false dichotomy, and traditionally spoke of 'etherialised matter'. Nolan seems to be on the right track. Where will he go next? If he would only stop making Batman films and get serious again, it would be interesting to see his next major work and track his progress further along the lines it seems to be taking. In this film we have 'three levels of dreaming' and we have 'the bottom of dreaming' which turns out to be another 'level of reality' which he calls Limbo, and describes as a 'confused mass' where some of the dead are stuck in a state of bewilderment. The density of the strange information presented in this film is too much for most viewers to grasp in a single viewing, nor is Nolan sufficiently explicit, but stops short in most cases with being merely suggestive, in order to keep his thriller moving right along. But what is really interesting about this film is not the story, but the background, assumptions, and context of the story. Nolan has thrown a huge indigestible 'confused mass' of Limbo at his viewers, and he needs to continue to untangle it and expound it in further works. This film therefore sweeps along and works in that sense, but it is far from being a perfect film, as it was too much to squeeze into a single story, despite all the best efforts of everyone concerned. We need to revisit these issues, as one film alone on this subject is not enough. After all, Batman has sequels, so why can't this one as well?

9.title: Highly Original Story
9.content:
Movies like this don't come along that often. Hollywood has come to realize that it is too risky to try and make money off an original idea. In their eyes, it is worth it to make a franchise reboot, or sequel, that is guaranteed to make money.

Director Christopher Nolan provides a breath of fresh air in today's movie scene, including an original story, quality performances, and a breathtaking score.

Inception is the story of Dom Cobb, a very skilled thief, who specializes in using a device to break into people's dreams and extract information. He is infamous for his type of crime and is on the run as the film begins. As the film progresses, the audience finds out that Cobb has been separated from his children for quite some time now, and will do anything to see them again. So, when someone offers him a job which could let him see his children again, he cannot decline. Brace yourself for a total mind trip as Cobb assembles a team to prepare for 'Inception.'

Initially, for a film that is about going into someone's dream and stealing information, it is entirely believable. The philosophy behind the film made me wonder, "Is this actually possible?" Nolan intentionally uses practical effects, something that is very rare to find in modern film. Most filmmakers rely heavily on CGI when they want an impossible shot, Nolan finds ways to do the impossible and excels at it. For example, there is a certain hallway scene in this movie that is 100% practical effects and is shocking how believable it is.

Inception is, quite literally, Nolan's dream. He originally wrote the screenplay while he was writing his first feature film, "Memento." The story isn't based off of a book, or any true events, it is imaginative fiction. It is one that has never been told before and that is what made this movie stand out to me. But no matter how good your effects, direction, or story may be, these don't make a movie, right?

Along with a stellar performance from Leonardo DiCaprio, other such as, Joseph Gordon Levitt, Ellen Page, and Tom Hardy all excel as their established characters. Needless to say, the acting in this movie is very convincing. The movie takes place in multiple different countries; so many of the characters have different dialects. Even with this language barrier, all of the characters still seemed to be coming from the same place and had great chemistry with one-another.

What you hear during a movie is said to be fifty percent of the experience, and Inception's score stands out from the crowd. Composer Han Zimmer and Christopher Nolan seem to always pair up and work together. Han provided the score for all of Nolan's "Dark Knight Trilogy," and 2014's "Interstellar." Zimmer's scores often get negative feedback regarding his 'power chords' and 'lack of emotion.' Despite this, I found his score to fit nicely with what Nolan was going for in the film. There is a very wide range of genre in the score, providing quiet, intimate moments, and all out action sequences.

All in all, Inception is a movie that proves Hollywood can make money with an original story. The performances bring you in, and the score takes you even deeper. You get immersed in the story and that is what makes this one of my favorite movies. Without a doubt, I would recommend this movie for anyone looking to sit down and have their mind blown.

9.title: Beyond human thinking
9.content:
I highly recommend Inception to everyone and I promise you won't be disappointed.

The story is about Dom Cobb is a man who enter people dreams to steal their secrets. But the twist is, Cobb is asked to plant an idea in someone's mind instead, which is called "inception." As the movie go on, the line between what real and what a dream starts to blur, and it hard to tell what happening. At first, I was really hooked by the action scenes and the amazing special effects. The dream worlds are

mind-blowing, especially when gravity changes or city fold in on themselves. It unlike anything I have ever seen before. The visual effects are stunning However, it becomes more complicated as the film progresses. The layers of dreams within dreams can be difficult to follow, and sometimes it feels like things are happening too fast to keep up. Hold on, what just took place? Was the question I asked myself. But that makes it more enjoyable. You want to fix the problem because it keeps you interested. I was trying to keep track of what was true and what wasn't, so I had to think a lot about the facts.

Even though all of the excitement, the film's emotional content was one thing that really caught my attention. Cobb's story is painful, since he recalls his wife, Mal. His fight with himself over her death is clear, and it serves as the main motivation for the whole film. His confusion and frustration are clear and I was able to relate to him on a deep level. His quest includes more than just his objective; it also involves his attempts to let go of the past.

I was both satisfied and confused after the end result. It's open-ended, and even after the film ended, I continued to think about it. Was Cobb awake? Was he still dreaming, or what? The film is so interesting because it doesn't provide a definitive answer. It is up to you to determine what is and is not real.

In the end, Inception is a film that tests your ability to think. It's a serious, thought-provoking movie about dreams, reality, and the power of our mind that goes beyond action and special effects. You can still learn new ideas from this type of movie even after seeing it a few times. I enjoyed how it forced me to think, despite the fact that I was sometimes confused. I will definitely be thinking about this film for a while.

9.title: Dream or reality
9.content:
My opinion of the film was very short, obviously I really liked the film, such a cast should be praised.

Let's find out how the film ended - There is no clear answer to the question of whether Cobb remained in a dream at the end of the film "Inception". The director deliberately did not give a clear answer to this question. According to one theory, Cobb did not pay attention to the top at the end, he no longer cared whether he was in the real world or in Limbo. He returned to his family, to his children, got rid of the burden of conscience for the death of his wife. On the other hand, actor Michael Caine, who plays Cobb's father, is sure that the ending of the film takes place in reality. He refers to the words of the director: "If you are filming a scene, then it is reality." As Christopher Nolan noted, the essence of the ending is that it does not matter whether the main character is in a dream or in reality. The point is that Cobb, after a difficult trial, finally found happiness and peace in the face of his children, with whom he can be both in a dream and in reality.

Personally, I am inclined to think that Cobb remained in a dream, this would be a more interesting ending, since Cobb does not care whether he is sleeping or not, the main thing is that he is happy.

9.title: a powerful film with a powerful concept.
9.content: Every once in a while a film finds its way across our screens that challenges us on several levels. Such films challenge us to think critically and pay attention. Others address issues that shake the core of human emotion. Additional films attack our senses with amazing visuals, a powerful score, or both. Christopher Nolan's Inception is a film that takes all of these elements in and turns them into a powerhouse of human emotion. The film explores the theme of the power of guilt and its subsequent ability to overtake everything that makes you yourself, while also making you question what the word reality truly means. The film stars the always powerful Leonardo DiCaprio as the films main protagonist Dom Cobb. Cobb is a man on the run from his past as well as from the country he calls home, struggling to cope with the loss of his wife and separation from his children. Cobb, along with Joseph Gordon-Levitt's character, Arthur, specialize in the extraction of memories from their victims' subconscious minds. Cobb and Arthur are so skilled at this job that they are invited by their most recent mark. The twist, it is revealed, is that he does not want a memory removed, rather he wants an idea inserted into another's mind; A job that is rewarded with nothing short of Cobb's return to his children. What ensues is Cobb's personal mission to accomplish the seemingly impossible and create perform inception on his intended mark. Inception is a film that utilizes both stunning visuals as well as Hans Zimmer's ever powerful score to navigate not only the gravity of the situations Cobb and company find themselves in, but also to explore the depth of emotion that the film resides in. Similar another seminal piece of Nolan film, Interstellar, Inception is a visual and musical delight that attacks the senses and connects the viewer(s) to the experience of the film. These films are also similar in the way that Nolan utilizes cinematography to address the theme of the film. Camera angles are a central focus in Inception, and Nolan uses them masterfully to shift focus from characters to more abstract items that help gain an attachment from his viewers on the concept of totems and their appearance. Inception is viewed by many as a masterpiece from Christopher Nolan. If begs the question of when reality stops being reality and when a dream stops being a dream. Inception also addresses the subconscious need for closure and acceptance of reality. This film stands to me as an excellent example of the power of film to excavate the deepest core feelings of the human mind and its ability to cope with its problems.

This is a really fun and complex thinkers film.

The plot, which moves between dream and reality, is defined as "a contemporary action science fiction film that takes place within the structure of consciousness". A dream maker, played by Leonardo dicaprio, leads a secret agent team played by Joseph Gordon-Levitt and Alan Page to enter other people's dreams, steal secrets from others' subconscious and reshape their dreams.

A lot of people don't understand the movie because they don't understand the dream, they don't know the nature of the dream. One of the best books to read about dreams is Freud's The Interpretation of Dreams.

Freud's description of the nature of dreams is "the true expression of inner desires". Dreams, in my view, are the direct reflection of the deepest desires of every human being.

Not only will there be one layer of dreams, but there will be dreams within dreams, as well as three and four layers of dreams. At each level of the dream, perceived time passes several times slower than real time. To wake from the next level of the dream, the act of death or falling must occur in the next level of the dream.

A lot of brain teasers aren't that brainy. It's just that the audience is too easily drawn into the muddle of the director's mind.
